findings.title: Exposure unit errors persist in emerging training data at the Part 1 rate (Part 1 fix 1 still applies); test files are clean
findings.evidence: Training rows whose exposure differs from (end-start+1)/365: buildings 153 (120 on a 360-day basis, 33 in days), contents 198 (164/34), motor 253 (206/47). That is 0.48-0.65% of rows in each year, against 0.59% in developed contents. Raw maximum is 365. Raw exposure totals are overstated: buildings 33,783 vs 23,468 clean (+44%), contents 38,893 vs 29,058 (+34%), motor 54,429 vs 38,969 (+40%). Test: 0 of 209,063 rows deviate.
findings.method: DuckDB comparison of exposure with (period_end-period_start+1)/365, /360 and day counts (tolerance 0.0006 years, or 0.5 days), by line, year and file.
findings.implication: With raw exposure, frequency and burning cost would be understated by about 25-30%. A few 365-unit rows would also dominate offsets in a book of only ~520 buildings claims a year.
findings.adjustment: Reuse the Part 1 rule as it stands: recompute exposure = (period_end-period_start+1)/365 on every training row and keep the raw value as exposure_raw. Add an assertion that the test files need no change.

check.note: I re-derived the counts with DuckDB by comparing exposure against (end-start+1)/365, /360 and a day count (tolerance 0.0006 years or 0.5 days). Rows that deviate: buildings 153 (120 on a 360-day basis, 33 in days), contents 198 (164/34), motor 253 (206/47). None fit neither pattern. By line and year the rate is 0.48-0.65%; developed contents is 0.59% (4,253 of 721,617). The raw maximum is 365. Raw against clean exposure: 33,783 vs 23,468 (+44%), 38,893 vs 29,058 (+34%), 54,429 vs 38,969 (+40%), so frequency is understated by 25-31%. The test files are clean: 0 of 209,063 rows deviate. One addition: almost all of the excess comes from the 114 rows recorded in days. They carry 10,342, 9,860 and 15,501 raw years against about 28, 27 and 42 clean years. The 360-day rows add only about 1.4% each. A day-count assertion therefore matters more than the 360-day fix.

findings.title: Sum insured x1,000 errors persist in both training and test (Part 1 fix 2 still applies, and the same thresholds work)
findings.evidence: Buildings: 53 training rows (0.19%) and 104 test rows (0.20%) from 60m to 568m, with nothing between 894k and 60m. Contents: 57 training and 135 test rows from 7.6m to 131.6m, with nothing between 283k and 7.6m. The same policy in another year shows a ratio of about 1,000: median 975 over 130 buildings pairs, 1,018 over 154 contents pairs. Premiums on flagged rows are normal (buildings 348.9 vs 357.5). Sum insured matters for severity: 12 of the 70 emerging buildings fire claims are 0.98-1.00x sum insured. The rate matches developed (0.20%).
findings.method: Quantiles and gap search on sum_insured by line and file. Self-join of policy-year maxima, flagged against unflagged years, for the ratio. Join of fire claims to their policy row.
findings.implication: 239 test rows would get predictions about 1,000x too high on any sum-insured term (log or tree), and 53 training rows would distort the fire and flood severity fit.
findings.adjustment: Divide by 1,000 where sum_insured >= 1m on both lines (Part 1's 1m contents and 10m buildings thresholds also separate cleanly here). Keep the raw value. Apply the rule identically to test.

check.note: The evidence holds. Flagged rows (sum insured of 1m or more): buildings 53 training (0.19%) and 104 test (0.20%), 60m-568m in total, with nothing between 894k and 60m. Contents 57 training (0.165%, not 0.20%) and 135 test (0.20%), 7.6m-131.6m, with nothing between 283k and 7.6m. Premiums on flagged buildings rows are 348.9 vs 357.5. The 239 test rows are correct, and both the 1m and 10m thresholds separate cleanly. The policy-pair ratios include test years: median 975 over 130 buildings pairs and 1,018 over 154 contents pairs. Training years alone give 1,027 over 49 and 981 over 54. Fire: 12 of 70 claims are at or above 0.98x sum insured, and 3 of these slightly exceed 1.00x (maximum 1.0004x). The implication is overstated. The 53 flagged buildings training rows carry 0 claims, and the 57 contents rows carry 1, so they cannot distort a fire or flood severity fit. Their harm in training is to frequency or burning-cost fits with a sum-insured term, where they add claim-free exposure at absurd values. The test-side harm, about 1,000x on 239 rows, stands.
check.corrected_evidence: Buildings: 53 training (0.19%) and 104 test (0.20%) rows from 60m to 568m, with nothing between 894k and 60m. Contents: 57 training (0.17%) and 135 test (0.20%) rows from 7.6m to 131.6m, with nothing between 283k and 7.6m. findings.implication: The target definition carries over unchanged. However, two years of emerging data cannot support their own development tail, and buildings and contents burning costs are dominated by a handful of large claims.
findings.adjustment: Keep the Part 1 period-match and repudiation filters, and keep dedup as a harmless step with an assertion of 0 removed. Use developed development factors by peril (lags are similar: bodily injury 135 vs 159 days, subsidence 80 vs 116). findings.title: Outcome leakage persists: customer_service_contacts and renewal_decision (Part 1 fixes 6 and 9 still apply)

findings.implication: Either field would make the training fit look excellent and then fail completely on test, where contacts carry no claim information.
findings.adjustment: Exclude both from every emerging model, as in Part 1. Add a guard that rejects any feature whose test mean matches the non-claimant subgroup rather than the training mean.

findings.title: year_built = 1900 placeholder persists (Part 1 fix 20 still applies)
findings.evidence: 4,421 addresses (3.2%) have year_built 1900, 10.6x the neighbouring years (about 385-420 a year from 1862 to 1905). Their energy ratings span A-G (A 600, B 693, C 714, D 644, E 501, F 414, G 334, missing 521). Genuine pre-1900 houses have no A or B ratings and only 6 at C. Buildings frequency for the 1900 group is 53 per 1,000 years: between post-1950 houses (31-35) and pre-1950 houses (63-68), as a mixture would be. The share is 3.1% of training rows and 3.2% of test rows (developed 3.3% of addresses).
findings.method: Count by year_built and its ratio to the mean of adjacent years. Cross-tab of energy rating by age group. Exposure-weighted buildings claim frequency by age group.
findings.implication: An age term would price these homes as Victorian, overstating subsidence, escape-of-water and fire risk on about 1,670 test buildings rows and the matching contents rows.
findings.adjustment: Apply the Part 1 fix: replace with the typical year built for the energy rating, keep the raw value plus a placeholder flag, and give the 521 with no energy rating a neutral age. The mapping can be estimated on emerging addresses, or taken from developed since the age-to-rating relationship looks the same.

check.note: Year 1900 covers 4,421 of 136,914 addresses (3.23%). That is 10.6x the adjacent years (419 each in 1899 and 1901) and 10.8x the mean of the five years either side (409). Years from 1862 to 1905 range from 380 to 466. Energy ratings for the 1900 group: A 600, B 693, C 714, D 644, E 501, F 414, G 334, missing 521. Genuine pre-1900 houses have no A or B ratings and 6 at C. Buildings frequency: 1900 group 53.1 per 1,000 years, pre-1900 67.8, 1901-49 62.8, 1950-79 36.3, 1980 onwards 31.7. Post-1950 is therefore 32-36, not 31-35. The share is 3.13% of training buildings rows and 3.20% of test rows (1,673 test buildings rows and 2,151 test contents rows); developed is 3.30% of addresses. Caveat: the 1900 frequency rests on 39 claims (95% interval about 38-73). It is close to the portfolio average of 45, so the mixture argument is weak on its own. The energy-rating evidence carries this finding.

findings.title: NEW: missing rates are about 5x Part 1 (about 12% against 2.5%) and look random, so Part 1's 'missing as its own level' relativities should not be carried over
findings.evidence: On the same 18 fields, about 12% are missing in emerging against about 2.5% in developed: days_unoccupied 12.0%, smoke_alarms 11.9%, high_value_items 11.8%, security_level 12.3%, engine_size_cc 12.2%, overnight_parking 12.1%, vehicle_age 11.9%, distance_to_river 12.0%, energy_rating 12.1%, roof_type, soil_type, household_size, marital_status, occupation and years_at_address 11.8-12.2%. Rates are the same in 2023, 2024 and the test files. flood_zone is unchanged (2.95% vs 2.92%). Joint motor missingness on 3 fields (0/1/2/3 missing: 68.0/28.1/3.75/0.14%) matches independence at 12% (68.1/27.9/3.8/0.17%), and does not vary with channel or new business (11.9-14.2%). Frequency barely differs between missing and present: motor parking 181 vs 181, engine size 186 vs 180, buildings smoke alarms 44 vs 45, contents security 32.5 vs 34.6 per 1,000. Missing flood zone does differ: 65 vs 44 per 1,000, but on only 43 claims.
findings.method: Null shares by field for each file and year in both markets. Distribution of the number of missing fields on a row, against a binomial. Exposure-weighted frequency split by missing flag.
findings.implication: About 32% of motor rows lack at least one of these three fields. A missing-level relativity or XGBoost default direction learned on developed data, where missingness was rarer and in flood zone informative (relativity 1.71), would misprice them.
findings.adjustment: For the about-12% fields, impute (mode or median, or the portfolio-average relativity) or set the missing level to base, rather than transferring developed missing-level coefficients. Keep flood zone missing as its own level, credibility-weighted towards the developed 1.71. Severity was not tested for missingness, so check it before finalising.

check.note: I computed null shares by field and file in both markets. Emerging fields run at 11.8-12.3% against 2.47-2.52% in developed, and flood zone is 2.95% vs 2.92%. The rates are stable across 2023, 2024 and 2025: motor 11.8-12.2% and buildings 11.6-12.2%. Joint motor missingness on engine size, parking and vehicle age, training rows: 68.0/28.1/3.75/0.14%, against a binomial at 12% of 68.1/27.9/3.8/0.17%. Missingness-weighted claim frequency per 1,000: parking 181.0 vs 180.8, engine size 186.2 vs 180.1, smoke alarms 44.1 vs 45.1, security 32.5 vs 34.6, flood zone 65.1 vs 44.4 (43 claims). Minor points: (1) Only 16 fields are shared: 15 at about 12% plus flood zone. Developed's 18 also include annual_mileage and telematics_score, which emerging lacks. (2) Missing shares by training channel and new business run 11.6-14.2%, and the 14.2% rests on 318 rows. (3) One exception was not reported: days_unoccupied missing runs at 35.4 vs 46.3 per 1,000 (100 claims, about 2.3 standard errors). Across 15 fields this is consistent with chance, but it deserves the same check as severity. Contents flood zone missing is 41.1 vs 34.1. The confidence level 'likely' is appropriate.

findings.title: NEW: occupation is corrupted into 80 raw values for 20 real occupations
findings.evidence: Emerging customers.occupation (135,856 customers): title case 43.8%, lower case 22.0%, trailing space 13.2%, a 'Self-employed ' prefix 8.8% (including impossible values such as 'Self-employed retired' 1,819, 'Self-employed student' 1,254 and 'Self-employed unemployed' 495), missing 12.2%. Developed has 20 clean values. The formats are spread identically across cohorts (72.5-73.7% of each format are 2025 customers), so this is not a broker-feed artefact. Motor frequency by format is 177-190 per 1,000, which is noise.
findings.method: Distinct counts before and after lower(trim()). Classification of formats by pattern. Join to developed occupations. Exposure-weighted motor frequency by format.
findings.implication: Used raw, occupation would split into 80 sparse levels. Developed occupation relativities would fail to match 44% of customers (50% of those with an occupation), which would fall silently to the default.
findings.adjustment: Normalise with lower(trim()), strip the 'self-employed ' prefix into a separate flag (test the flag; drop it if it adds nothing, which looks likely), and map to the 20 developed levels. Treat missing as above.

check.note: There are 80 distinct raw values. lower(trim()) reduces them to 40, and stripping the prefix to 20, which match the 20 developed values. By format, over 135,856 customers: title case 43.8%, lower case 22.0%, trailing space 13.2%, 'Self-employed ' prefix 8.8%, missing 12.2%. The impossible combinations number 1,819 (retired), 1,254 (student) and 495 (unemployed). The 2025-cohort share by format is 72.5-73.7%. Exact match to developed values: 43.8% of all customers and 49.8% of those with an occupation, so 44% of customers (50% of non-missing) would fail to match. Motor claims per 1,000 by format range from 176.8 to 190.1, with the prefixed format highest on 640 claims, about 1.4 standard errors above the rest. This is noise, as stated.

findings.title: Construction codes are recoded between markets, not between years. Part 1 fixes 3 (mixed case) and 18 (timber T->W) no longer apply, but a mapping is needed
findings.evidence: Emerging buildings use only BRK, MIX, STN and WOD, all upper case, with shares identical in 2023, 2024 and 2025 (BRK 69.7/70.1/70.2%). Developed still has 9 mixed-case variants. Shares imply BRK=brick (69.9 vs 70.0%), MIX=non_standard (10.1 vs 9.9%), STN=stone (7.9 vs 8.0%), WOD=timber (12.0 vs 12.1%). Frequency per 1,000 ranks the same way (developed 2023-24 in brackets): MIX 72 (non_standard 58), WOD 49 (timber 45.5), BRK 40.7 (brick 42.7), STN 41.3 (stone 43.0). A year-by-year scan of every text and boolean policy field across the three lines found no 2023-to-2024 or 2024-to-2025 recode. Only new_business share (expected) and renewal_decision (training-only) differ.
findings.method: Value counts by year and file for every VARCHAR and BOOLEAN policy field, flagging levels absent in a year or with share ratios above 2.5. Share and frequency comparison against developed construction after Part 1's cleaning.
findings.implication: Any Part 1 relativity keyed on 'brick', 'timber' or 'non_standard' would match none of the emerging rows and fall to a default for every row. MIX is the highest-frequency class and would be underpriced.
findings.adjustment: Add an explicit mapping (BRK->brick, STN->stone, WOD->timber, MIX->non_standard) with an assertion of no unmapped levels. Keep the raw code. Treat the MIX->non_standard link as inferred, so re-estimate its relativity on emerging data or test it.

check.note: Emerging codes are BRK, MIX, STN and WOD only. BRK runs 69.7/70.1/70.2% in 2023/2024/2025, MIX 10.2/10.0/10.0%, STN 7.9/7.9/7.9% and WOD 12.1/12.0/12.0%. Developed after cleaning: brick 70.0%, non_standard 9.9%, stone 8.0%, timber 12.1%. Buildings claims per 1,000: MIX 72.1, WOD 49.1, STN 41.3, BRK 40.7. Developed 2023-24: non_standard 58.4, timber 45.5, stone 43.0, brick 42.7. I scanned every VARCHAR and BOOLEAN field in the three lines by year and file. No level is absent in any year, and the only share ratio above 2.5 is new_business. Wording: developed has 11 raw construction values for 4 classes (Brick, BRICK, brick, NON_STANDARD, non_standard, STONE, stone, T, t, W, w), not '9 mixed-case variants'. Stone sits marginally above brick in both markets, which is noise. The MIX to non_standard mapping is an inference, so 'likely' is right.

findings.title: NEW: identifiers collide between the two markets, so pooled or reused Part 1 joins would silently attach developed data to emerging test rows
findings.evidence: All 137,804 emerging motor row_ids (47,283 training plus 90,521 test) and 36,104 of the 52,295 emerging buildings test row_ids are the same strings as developed training row_ids. Developed motor runs [id]-[id]; emerging motor runs [id]-[id]. Other overlaps: 621 policy_ids, 19 claim_ids, 752 customer_ids (only 4 with the same surname, so different people), 8,046 address_ids and all 987 emerging repairer_ids. Within emerging, all IDs are unique.
findings.method: Joins of distinct ID sets between the emerging and developed tables, file by file.
findings.implication: 126,625 of the 209,063 test rows (61%) could pick up a developed target, feature or weather record if the Part 1 SQL, which is keyed on row_id, customer_id and address_id, is run over pooled tables or against cached developed outputs. The error would be silent, and severe.
findings.adjustment: Namespace every key by market (for example 'E_' or 'D_') before any union, assert key uniqueness after pooling, and never join the emerging tables to developed tables or caches by ID.

check.note: All 47,283 emerging training and 90,521 test motor row_ids appear among developed training row_ids, as do 36,104 of the 52,295 test buildings row_ids. Contents has none. Developed motor training runs [id]-[id], and emerging motor [id]-[id]. Other overlaps: 621 policy_ids, 19 claim_ids, 752 customer_ids (4 with the same surname), 8,046 address_ids, all 987 repairer_ids and also 10 third_party_ids. Within emerging, all 318,359 row_ids are unique, as are the customer, address and claim IDs. The row_id overlap alone covers 126,625 of 209,063 test rows (60.6%). Counting any collision on row_id, customer_id or address_id raises this to 131,946 (63.1%), so the 61% is a lower bound.

findings.title: NEW: tenure fields contradict the two-year market history, and new business, 76% of 2025, is thin and differently timed in training
findings.evidence: In 2023, the insurer's first year in the market, 88% of rows are renewals with a mean renewal_count of 8.0 (range 1-15). 27,433 customers (20%) have customer_since_year 2008-2022. Every 2023 policy (47,173 across the lines) reappears in 2024, and 2023 has no cancelled or lapsed decisions, against 4.9% and 9.8% in 2024; even the 181 declined_by_insurer policies reappear. Developed 2021, its first data year, shows the same artefact. Coding is consistent in test: new business if and only if renewal_count = 0, all test-only customers have customer_since_year 2025, and new business never ends early in training or test. New business is 7.7-7.8% of clean training exposure (1,810, 2,233 and 3,040 years; 77, 102 and 697 claims) against 76% of test rows. Motor new business runs at 229 vs 177 claims per 1,000 and 620 vs 389 cost per exposure-year; contents 45.7 vs 33.4. Training new business incepts evenly through the year (mean exposure 0.47), whereas 60,769 of 68,823 test motor new-business rows incept on 2-15 January (about 4,300 a day).
findings.method: Policy continuity by self-join on policy_id across consecutive years. Cross-tab of renewal_decision against next-year presence. Profile of customer_since_year. Frequency and cost per exposure by new_business on Part 1 cleaned targets (undeveloped). Inception-date distribution.
findings.implication: renewal_count and customer_since cannot mean experience with this insurer here, and 2023 is a survivor cohort with no mid-term exits. The new-business loading that will drive about 76% of 2025 cost rests on under 900 emerging claims and is confounded with inception month.
findings.adjustment: Treat tenure fields as given attributes rather than evidence of claims history with this insurer, and use claim-history credibility only for the 24% of 2025 renewals. Estimate the new-business effect with a seasonality or inception-month control, credibility-weighted towards the developed new-business relativity. Report it as a named source of uncertainty.

check.note: These hold: 2023 is 88.1% renewals, with a mean renewal_count of 8.0 among renewals (range 1-15). 27,433 customers (20.2%) have a customer_since_year of 2008-2022. All 47,173 policies from 2023 reappear in 2024, including the 181 declined_by_insurer. 2023 has no cancelled or lapsed policies, and developed 2021 shows the same pattern. New business holds exactly when renewal_count = 0 in training and test. All 99,088 test-only customers have a customer_since_year of 2025. No new-business policy ends before year end. New business is 7.7-7.8% of clean exposure (1,810, 2,233 and 3,040 years; 77, 102 and 697 claims) against 76.0% of test rows. Motor new business runs at 229 vs 177 claims per 1,000 and 620 vs 389 cost per exposure-year; contents 45.7 vs 33.4. Training new business has a mean exposure of 0.47. Corrections: (1) In 2024, cancelled is 4.9% and lapsed 9.6% of rows across all lines. The 9.8% is buildings alone; on a policy basis the figures are 5.2% and 10.2%. (2) 60,374 of 68,823 test motor new-business rows incept on 2-15 January (87.7%, about 4,300 a day), not 60,769. (3) Buildings runs the other way: new business 42.5 vs 45.2 per 1,000 and 338 vs 413 cost per exposure-year, on 77 claims. The new-business effect is not uniformly upward, so a single developed new-business loading should not be applied across lines. Another point: 167 of the 181 policies declined_by_insurer in 2024 reappear in the 2025 test file, so declines are not exits either.

findings.title: Part 1 fixes that no longer apply, and Part 1 'leave as recorded' items that still hold
findings.evidence: No longer needed: (a) customer_id padding: all 135,856 IDs have 8 characters and 100% of 318,359 policy rows join without padding. (b) Region R11 elevation in feet: there is no R11; all six E regions cap at 60.0 m with medians of 7.4-7.6 m, the same as developed regions other than R11; flood zone and river distance are consistent by region. (c) Constant-ratio unit errors: none across E01-E06 for any numeric address, policy or claim field. Only weather (rainfall 0.84-1.31x, wildfire 0.67-1.57x) differs by region, and its ratios are not constant, which points to climate rather than units. (d) Licensed before 16: 0 rows exceed the maximum years licensed implied by the driver's age band (the band maxima found are 7, 17, 32 and 47; Part 1 had 3,717). (e) Zero mileage and telematics: the fields are absent. (f) Joins: every row joins to its address and to same-year weather (136,914 addresses x 2023-2025, no duplicates), with no overlapping periods and 18,633 mid-term splits all contiguous. Still holds: (g) written premium is annual (correlation with exposure -0.004 to -0.031 in training, -0.020 to 0.010 in test). findings.title: Test against training: coding is consistent, but the mix and the 2025 weather move outside the training range
findings.evidence: Every 2025 categorical level appears in 2023-24, numeric test ranges lie within training, and the 20 reference_policies match their test rows exactly on all 25, 26 and 34 shared fields. Mix shifts: drivers and policyholders aged 17-34 are 50% of test against 38-40% of training, and the median years licensed is 13 against 24. In 2025 weather, mean freezing days are 28.9 against 19.3 in training, and 10.4% of address-years fall outside the training p1-p99 for freezing days, 14.0% for rainfall and 10.9% for temperature (the 2025 minimum temperature is 9.6 against a training minimum of 10.3). Separately, the expenses table has no emerging comparison-site commission (NaN), although 10,458 test rows (5.0%) and 5,471 training rows come through that channel.
findings.method: Level scan by file and year. Numeric min, p1, p50, p99 and max by file. Field-by-field equality of reference_policies against test rows. Weather quantiles for 2025 against the 2023-24 training range.
findings.implication: No coding fix is needed for test. However, weather and young-driver terms will be extrapolated for about 10-14% of address-years, and the comparison-site expense gap affects pricing, though not the claim-cost target.
findings.adjustment: Clip weather covariates to the training p1-p99 range (or use smooth terms with linear tails) and flag the extrapolated share in the uncertainty write-up. Stress-test the young-driver relativities against developed. For pricing only, state an assumption for comparison-site commission (for example, the developed 10%).

check.note: These hold: every 2025 categorical level appears in 2023-24. The 20 reference_policies (7 buildings, 6 contents, 7 motor) match their test rows on all 25, 26 and 34 shared fields. 17-34s are 50.2%, 49.9% and 50.0% of test against 39.0%, 38.7% and 39.1% of training, and median years licensed is 13 against 24. 2025 freezing days average 28.9 against 19.3. Shares of 2025 address-years outside the training p1-p99 range: 10.4% (freezing), 14.0% (rainfall), 10.9% (temperature). The minimum temperature is 9.6 against 10.3. Comparison-site commission is NaN, covering 10,458 test rows (5.0%) and 5,471 training rows. Corrections: (1) Numeric test ranges are not wholly within training. The test maxima are slightly higher: buildings sum insured 894k vs 813k, contents 283k vs 235k, missed_payments 7 vs 5, vehicle_age 27 vs 26, renewal_count 17 vs 16. This is consistent with a larger sample one year older, not a coding problem. (2) Extrapolation is overstated. By construction, 1.7-2.0% of training address-years lie outside these p1-p99 bounds. Only 0.09% (freezing), 0.40% (rainfall) and 0.04% (temperature) of 2025 address-years fall outside the training minimum and maximum. 2025 is a level shift into the sparse tails: colder and drier, with rainfall 1,251 vs 1,378, temperature 14.2 vs 15.5 and hail 11.4 vs 15.5. Clipping at p1-p99 would change 10-14% of 2025 values and damp a real weather signal. Clipping at the training minimum and maximum is the targeted fix. (3) The young-driver shift is entirely new-business mix, not extrapolation. Training new business is 54.1% aged 17-34 with a median of 10 years licensed, the same as test new business (53.6%, 10). Renewals are 36.6% (25) in training and 39.2% (23) in test. The risk lies in the credibility of thin new-business young-driver data, not in age ranges beyond the data. findings.title: The 2025 book is about 3.9 times the 2024 exposure and 77% new business; none of the new business has been seen before
findings.evidence: Exposure from dates: motor 79,007 in the test against 20,104 in 2024 (x3.93), buildings 47,376 against 12,095 (x3.92), contents 59,016 against 14,950 (x3.95). New-business share of exposure is 76.9% / 76.8% / 77.0% in 2025, against 9.1% in 2024 and 7.8% over 2023-24 (by rows it is 76% against 12.1% in 2023 and 15.3% in 2024). Every test row with new_business=False is a 2024 policy renewing: 100% of its policy and customer IDs appear in training, and 100% of 2024 rows that ran to year end, 'renewed' or 'declined_by_insurer', are in the test. Every test row with new_business=True is a customer never seen on any line (0.0%), and only 0.6% (buildings), 1.2% (contents) and 2.2% (motor) sit at a previously insured address. The renewal book is not adversely selected: retained 2024 motor policies claimed 173 per 1,000 against 179 for those that lapsed, and claimants were retained more often (89% against 81%), the same pattern as in the developed market.
findings.method: DuckDB joins of test against training on policy_id, customer_id and address_id; exposure recomputed as (period_end - period_start + 1)/365; 2024 rows collapsed to policy level and retention cut by claim flag.
findings.implication: The 2025 prediction is dominated by business with no internal history. A new-business relativity applies to 77% of exposure, against under 10% in any fitting year, so a small error in that relativity becomes a material error in the level. The 2025 total is roughly four times any year the model was fitted on.
findings.adjustment: Treat new business as an explicit segment. Report and validate the predicted level separately for new business and renewals, and size the uncertainty mainly on the new-business segment.

check.note: Re-derived with DuckDB from period dates, ID joins of test against training, and 2024 rows collapsed to policy level. Exposure: motor 79,007 against 20,104 (x3.93), buildings 47,376 against 12,095 (x3.92), contents 59,016 against 14,950 (x3.95). New-business share of exposure: 76.9%, 76.8% and 77.0%, against 9.1% in 2024 and 7.7-7.8% over 2023-24. Row shares (motor): 76.0% against 12.1% in 2023 and 15.3% in 2024. All test renewals have a policy and customer seen in training. New business: 0.0% of customers seen before; 0.6%, 1.2% and 2.2% at a previously insured address. Every 2024 row that ran to year end as renewed or declined_by_insurer is in the test (20,097 motor, 12,103 buildings, 14,922 contents). Motor frequency: retained 173.2 per 1,000 against 178.5 for lapsed. One precision point: the 89% against 81% retention split is for 2024 renewal policies only (89.3% against 80.8%). Across all 2024 policies it is 90.5% against 83.9%, because every 2024 new-business policy and every 2023 policy was retained. The developed market gives 89.3% against 81.2%. Facts worth adding: the only observable lapse is on 2024 renewals, so the retention evidence covers one year; and policies declined_by_insurer still appear in the 2025 test, which is a data oddity.

findings.title: The broker portfolio cannot be told apart from 2023-24 organic new business on any observed factor, and the channel field does not identify it
findings.evidence: PSI of 2025 new business against 2023-24 new business, over every policy, customer and address field, is at most 0.033 (written premium 0.033, occupation 0.031). The only exceptions are customer_since_year (2025 against 2023/24, by construction) and customer_service_contacts, which is the known leakage field. Channel mix is 70.0% broker, 25.0% direct and 5.0% comparison site in 2025 new business, against 70.2/25.0/4.9 across training. Region, urban density, payment method, cover type, sum insured, flood zone, property type, multi-line holding (70% of buildings customers also hold contents at the same address, about 40% hold motor) and prior_claims_5y all match training to within 1 percentage point (PSI <= 0.002).
findings.method: Exposure-weighted and row-weighted share tables by group (developed 2024, developed test, emerging training split into renewals and new business, emerging test split the same way). PSI on decile bins of the emerging training distribution; categoricals taken as they are.
findings.implication: On observables, the 2025 shift is more new business, not a different kind of new business. The 6,535 motor, 3,786 buildings and 4,716 contents new-business rows in training are therefore a representative sample of the broker book, and relativities estimated on them should transfer. Any way the broker portfolio is genuinely different (broker selection, anti-selection on transfer) is invisible in the data and can only be handled as an assumption.
findings.adjustment: Do not create a broker-portfolio factor from channel; it carries no signal for this. Give a broker-selection load (for example plus or minus 5-10% on new business) as an explicit sensitivity in the uncertainty statement, not as a point adjustment.

check.note: The conclusion stands: 2025 new business cannot be told apart from 2023-24 new business on any observable, and channel does not identify the broker book. Two of the stated bounds are literally wrong, though the excesses are immaterial. Calculated by PSI on training-new-business deciles, row and exposure weighted, plus share tables. Channel and multi-line holding are confirmed. That training new business is representative of the broker book remains an inference.

findings.title: The mix shift comes from younger, less experienced customers; everything else is flat
findings.evidence: Exposure shares in the 2025 new-business book against emerging training (developed 2024 in brackets): age 17-24 27.8% against 19.6% (13.5%); under 35, 50.3% of the whole test book against 38.3% (32.7%); young_* marketing segments 51.3% against 33.0% (27.2%); motor years licensed <= 1, 19.2% against 13.0% (4.0%); NCB 0-2 years 41.3% against 32.2% (17.5%); third party only plus third party fire and theft 22.8% against 21.1%. Mean motor written premium is 700 for new business against 601 for 2024 renewals. Every other factor has PSI < 0.01. The 2025 renewals are the 2024 book one year older: years licensed <= 1 falls from 12.2% to 3.0%, NCB 0 from 9.1% to 5.0%, and vehicles aged <= 5 from 8.8% to 1.2%. First-order decomposition of the motor frequency index (emerging Poisson GLM): new-business book +9.7% (years licensed +7.3, NCB +3.8, cover type -1.7, others under 1); renewal book -8.6%. In the home lines the shift sits in age band combined with marketing segment, which are collinear (for example contents capped cost: age +26%, segment -17%, net +6.7%).
findings.method: Share tables as above. Poisson (frequency) and Tweedie p=1.5 (claims capped at 50k) GLMs fitted on emerging 2023-24 with an exposure weight, about 20 shared factors and no new-business term. Each factor's contribution is the difference in exposure-weighted mean linear predictor between test group and training.
findings.implication: Age, years licensed and NCB carry the 2025 level change, so their curves are the relativities that matter most to carry over or to re-estimate. Region and channel relativities hardly move the 2025 level, although they still matter row by row. Read age band and segment jointly, never one at a time.
findings.adjustment: Keep years licensed, NCB, age band and segment in every line's model, and score the 2025 rows through the model rather than carrying a 2024 average level forward.

check.note: The direction holds: young and inexperienced drivers carry the 2025 new-business shift, and renewals age. Mix-share figures confirmed: age 17-24 27.8% against 19.6% (13.5%); under 35 50.3% against 38.2% (32.6%); young segments 51.3% against 33.0% (27.2%); years licensed <= 1 19.2% against 13.0% (4.0%); NCB 0-2 41.3% against 32.3% (17.5%); TPO/TPFT 22.8% against 21.1%; written premium 700 against 601.

findings.implication: A properly specified model picks this up automatically. A level calibrated to the 2023-24 or 2024 average and applied flat would understate 2025 motor by 7-10% and contents by about 5-7% before trend, inflation or any new-business effect.

findings.title: New business carries a residual relativity of about 1.10-1.13 that the observed factors do not explain; Part 1's GLMs do not include it

findings.implication: Under-predicting new business at 77% of exposure moves the whole level. Apply it flat across ages.

findings.title: In 2023-24 the emerging book's mix aged, which makes a raw year-on-year change look like trend
findings.evidence: Observed motor frequency fell from 188.6 to 173.6 per 1,000 between 2023 and 2024 (-7.9%). Model-predicted frequency on observed factors fell from 184.6 to 177.5 (-3.8%), so about half the fall is mix; A/E moved from 1.022 to 0.979, leaving about -4.2% for development plus true trend. Capped motor cost per exposure: observed -10.5%, mix -5.3%. New-business inflow of 12-15% of rows does not replace the young and low-NCB drivers who age out each year, so the 2025 renewals score a further -12% (index 0.883). Buildings and contents mix changed by under 1% a year.
findings.method: Emerging GLM without year or new-business terms, scored by policy year; A/E = observed / predicted.
findings.implication: An emerging-only trend fitted on raw 2023-24 frequency would be biased downwards, by about 4 points for motor, and would be wrongly projected onto a 2025 book whose mix moves the other way.
findings.adjustment: Estimate any emerging trend net of rating factors and after development, or carry the developed trend over (motor +3.8%, contents +4.2%, buildings +5.3%) unless there is market-specific evidence against it.

findings.title: Claim-history credibility reaches only 23% of 2025 exposure, while the customer-declared prior_claims_5y covers everyone and carries over well
findings.evidence: Of 2025 test rows, 24% have any internal history, and at most 2023-24 (claims dated 2021-22 are 33 in total). Rows with an own-line prior claim: motor 23.1% of renewals, so 5.5% of the whole test book; buildings 7.1% of renewals; contents 5.4%. In the developed 2025 test, renewals are 85% of the book and 27% of motor renewals have an own-line prior claim. Emerging 2023 rows have no history at all, so k cannot be tuned on emerging as Part 1 tuned it on 2023. prior_claims_5y is populated for all rows and its distribution is the same in 2025 new business (77% zero). One-way frequency relativities for 1 and 2+ prior claims, emerging against developed 2023-24: motor 1.24 / 1.74 against 1.26 / 1.56; buildings 1.13 / 1.53 against 1.30 / 1.74; contents 1.20 / 1.54 against 1.24 / 1.61.
findings.method: Customer-level count of non-repudiated pre-2025 claims joined to test rows; one-way frequency by prior_claims_5y (capped at 2) on reported claims.
findings.implication: Part 1's credibility factor is almost irrelevant to the 2025 level and cannot stand in for the new-business effect: new-business rows get the neutral factor of 1 even though their risk is about 12% higher. If it is rebalanced 'so fitted rows keep their total' on a training book that is 92% renewals, the constant is set by renewals and new business is under-priced by the missing step.
findings.adjustment: Apply credibility to renewals only, with Part 1's k values (short window, so expect factors close to 1), and rebalance within renewals. Carry prior_claims_5y as the history signal for everyone, with the developed relativity as a prior. Price new business through the explicit new-business factor, not through credibility.

check.note: Calculated from distinct customers with non-repudiated, in-period, pre-2025 own-line claims, joined to test rows, plus one-way frequency by prior_claims_5y capped at 2. Renewals are 24.0% of 2025 test rows and 23.1% of exposure. Motor: 23.1% of renewals have an own-line prior claim, 5.5% of the whole book. Matching home lines on customer only gives buildings 7.1% and contents 5.4%. Part 1's own-line key for home (customer and address) gives 6.4% and 4.9% (1.5% and 1.2% of the book). Developed test: 84.8% renewals, 27.1% of motor renewals with history. Pre-2023 claims: 34, not 33, all closed and none inside any policy period, so 2023 rows have no history. prior_claims_5y is fully populated, with 77.2% zero in 2025 new business against 76.8% in training. The one-way relativities reproduce exactly: motor 1.24/1.74 against 1.26/1.56; buildings 1.13/1.53 against 1.30/1.74; contents 1.20/1.54 against 1.24/1.61. Training is 92% renewals by exposure. That rebalancing under-prices new business is a sound inference.

findings.title: The tenure fields contradict the 'two years in market' narrative and behave as new-business proxies; customer_since_year for 2025 new business is outside the training range
findings.evidence: In 2023, the first year of writing, 87.9% of rows are renewals, renewal_count runs evenly from 1 to 15+ (about 5.4% at each value), and 23,758 customers have customer_since_year before 2021 (back to 2008). campaign_code is populated if and only if customer_since_year >= 2023 in emerging (>= 2021 in developed): 93.6% missing for training renewals, 0% for new business. customer_since_year is 2025 for 100% of 2025 new business, against a training maximum of 2024. discount_applied is fixed by channel and new business together (direct 5%, comparison-site new business 10%, otherwise 0). Part 1's XGBoost permitted list includes customer_since_year, campaign_code, renewal_count, new_business and discount_applied.
findings.method: Cross-tabulations of renewal_count, customer_since_year, campaign_code and discount against new_business and channel, emerging and developed.
findings.implication: Fact: within the data, new_business is a clean 'new to this book' flag. Inference: the 2023 renewals behave like an acquired or seasoned book, so renewal_count is not tenure in this market. Tree models fed the raw customer_since_year will treat 2025 as the same as 2024 (no extrapolation), which is benign only by accident. Several fields are duplicate encodings of new business, and in a GLM they would split or distort its relativity.
findings.adjustment: Use one new-business indicator, or tenure = policy year - customer_since_year capped at 1. Drop raw customer_since_year, campaign_code presence and discount_applied as separate factors for emerging, and do not use renewal_count beyond the 0/1+ split.

check.note: Cross-tabulations reproduce. 2023 rows: 87.9% renewals. renewal_count is 0 for 12.1% of rows, and each value from 1 to 15+ holds 5.5-6.2% (about 5.9%, not 5.4%; immaterial). 23,758 customers have customer_since_year before 2021, back to 2008, and all are in training. campaign_code is populated exactly when customer_since_year >= 2023 in emerging and >= 2021 in developed, with no exceptions. It is missing for 93.6% of motor training renewals (38,133 of 40,748) and 0% of new business. customer_since_year equals the policy year exactly when new_business is true, in every year of both markets: 2025 for 100% of 2025 new business, against a training maximum of 2024. Discount is 5% for direct, 10% for comparison-site new business and 0 otherwise, with no exceptions. Part 1's XGBoost raw and line lists include customer_since_year, campaign_code, renewal_count, new_business and discount_applied. That the 2023 renewals behave like a seasoned or acquired book is an inference.

findings.title: 2025 new business starts in January for a full year, while training new business is spread through the year and less developed
findings.evidence: Day of the year at inception, 2025 new business: 10th percentile 3, median 9, 75th percentile 13, 90th percentile 82; mean exposure 0.88. Training new business: median 193 (10th to 90th percentile 41-332), mean exposure 0.47. The developed market is the same as emerging training (median 192-193). Emerging new-business-over-renewal A/E on frequency by policy year: 2023 1.227 (95% CI 1.09-1.38), 2024 1.071 (0.96-1.19). The 2024 new-business exposure is concentrated late in 2024, so its claims are the least developed at the 31 December 2024 valuation.
findings.method: Quantiles of extract(doy from period_start); A/E ratio from the emerging GLM without a new-business term, with log-normal intervals from claim counts.
findings.implication: The emerging new-business relativity measured on reported claims is biased downwards, mostly in 2024. The test book's timing differs from training's: contents seasonal weights barely matter for full-year rows, and any new-business 'first months on cover' effect is spread over a full year in 2025 against half a year in training.
findings.adjustment: Estimate the new-business relativity on developed-to-ultimate claims, or weight towards policy year 2023 and the developed market. Use full-year exposure for the 2025 new-business rows (already in the test data) and check the seasonal-exposure treatment does not double count.

check.note: Timing: 2025 new-business inception day of year for motor is p10 3, median 9, p75 13, p90 82 (buildings p90 15, contents 30); mean exposure 0.88-0.92. The downward bias is real but about 3-5% on the 2024 relativity (about 2% pooled), far smaller than the 2023-to-2024 swing of about 17%, which is mostly noise. Developed shows the same 2024 dip (motor 1.093 to 1.022). Precision point: 2024 new business is not timed later than 2023's (median day 191 against 196). It is late relative to renewals in both years, and only 2024's is close to the valuation date.

findings.title: How the emerging book differs from the developed one: channel, driver experience, vehicles, missing data and code sets
findings.evidence: Emerging training against developed 2024 (exposure shares). Channel: broker 70.2% against 25.0%, comparison site 4.9% against 35.0%, direct 25.0% against 40.0%. The expenses table has no comparison-site commission for emerging, although 4.9% of rows use that channel. Electric vehicles 2.0% against 8.0%; vehicles aged <= 5 years 8.9% against 21.4%; NCB 0-2 32.2% against 17.5%; years licensed <= 1 13.0% against 4.0%; age 17-24 19.6% against 13.5%; clay soil 34.8% against 41.6%. Missing values run at about 12% per field (vehicle age, engine size, parking, occupation, distance to river, soil, roof, energy rating, days unoccupied, security, high-value items) against 2.5%, so 84-86% of emerging rows have at least one missing field against 62-63%; missingness rates are the same for new business and renewals. Construction codes BRK/MIX/STN/WOD hold 69.9/10.2/7.8/12.1%, matching developed brick/non-standard/stone/timber at 70.0/10.0/7.9/12.1%. Occupation has up to four spellings per job (case and trailing-space variants) plus a 'Self-employed' prefix. Regions E01-E06 do not overlap R01-R12. The sum-insured x1000 error recurs (rows >= 1m: 104 buildings and 135 contents test rows). Raw exposure is again wrong on training rows (buildings 2023 raw mean 1.49 against 0.90 from dates); the test files are clean.
findings.method: Share and PSI tables, emerging training against developed 2024; null-rate profile by group; value counts.
findings.implication: These are level and relativity differences between markets, not part of the 2025 shift (none differs between 2025 new business and training). They limit what carries over: region cannot carry over at all; channel, and especially comparison site, rests on thin emerging data; Part 1's missing-value levels will cover about 12% of rows, not 2.5%, so their relativities matter more.
findings.adjustment: Map construction codes one-to-one; normalise occupation (lower case, trim, strip the prefix into a self-employed flag) or leave it out; apply the Part 1 sum-insured and exposure fixes; re-estimate region from emerging data with shrinkage; check that missing-value relativities hold in emerging before carrying them over.

findings.title: Driver and policyholder age, the main shift driver, can be reconstructed beyond the bands
findings.evidence: Developed motor: corr(driver_age, years_licensed) = 0.993, and driver_age - years_licensed lies between 17 and 25 for 98% of rows (median 21). Emerging years licensed by band is consistent with this: 17-24 has median 1 and 99th percentile 7; 65+ has median 57. Marketing-segment life stage is a strict function of age in the developed data: young 17-31, midlife 31-51, mature 51-71, senior 71-91. In emerging, 'senior' is entirely 65+ and 'young' entirely under 35. In the emerging motor frequency GLM, driver_age_band relativities are flat (0.97-1.03) once years licensed and NCB are in, so motor age risk sits in years licensed.
findings.method: Correlation and quantiles of age minus years licensed in developed; cross-tabulation of segment life stage against age band in both markets; GLM coefficients.
findings.implication: Part 1's age curves (driver-age spline, policyholder-age spline) can be carried over through an imputed age, not lost to banding. That matters because age and experience drive the 2025 mix shift. Banding alone would blur the 17-24 group, which grows from 19.6% to 27.8% in new business.
findings.adjustment: For motor, impute age = clip(years_licensed + 21, band limits), or simply rely on the years licensed and NCB curves. For home lines, refine the band with segment life stage (for example 25-34 young = 25-31, 65+ senior = 71+). Check with an emerging A/E by refined band before relying on it.

check.note: Reconstructing age is sound. Segment life stage, however, is not a strict function of age, so one proposed refinement is wrong. Age-band flatness holds on an A/E basis but not as fitted coefficients when segment is in the model. Calculated by correlation and quantiles on developed motor, cross-tabs of segment by age, and A/E by age band from my emerging Poisson GLMs without an age term.
check.corrected_evidence: Developed: corr(driver_age, years_licensed) = 0.9935. Age minus years licensed lies in 17-25 for 99.4% of rows (not 98%), median 21. Emerging years licensed: 17-24 band median 1, p99 6, maximum 7; 65+ median 57. Developed segment age ranges overlap by about 3 years at each boundary: young 17-31, midlife 28-51, mature 48-71, senior 68-91; the crossover is about 30, 50 and 70 (at age 70: 9,082 senior against 3,282 mature). So '65+ senior = 71+' is wrong: senior starts at about 68, mostly 70+, and 65+ mature is about 65-71. '25-34 young = 25-31' holds; 25-34 midlife is about 28-34. In emerging, senior is all 65+ and young is all under 35 (confirmed). Motor age band: A/E by age band from a model with years licensed, NCB and segment but no age band is 0.99-1.00; without segment it is 0.95-1.02 (50-64 at 0.95). If age band and segment are fitted together, the age coefficients are 1.08-1.48 against 65+, because the two are collinear. Age band therefore adds little beyond years licensed, NCB and segment, but its coefficients are not 'flat (0.97-1.03)' in every specification.

findings.title: Emerging loss cost is 0.75 to 0.91 of developed, and the frequency and severity parts behave differently on each line
findings.evidence: Ultimate cost per unit of exposure for 2023-24 combined, with a 90% bootstrap range for sampling error only: buildings 415.8 (351-489), contents 88.9 (80-98), motor 445.0 (421-472). The Part 1 documented ultimates (s3.5) for the same years average 459.3 for buildings, 118.6 for contents and 582.9 for motor, or about 553 without the 11.89m claim. Ratios: buildings 0.91, contents 0.75, motor 0.80 (0.76 including the 11.89m claim). Breakdown: buildings frequency 45.0 against 44.6 per 1,000, but buildings excluding fire is 0.64 of developed loss cost (230.5 against about 360) at equal frequency (42.0 against 42.7); contents frequency 34.3 against 40.5 (x0.85) with mean severity x0.89; motor ultimate frequency 184 against 137 per 1,000 (x1.34) with severity about 2,420 against 4,030 (x0.60). The 2025 test exposure is 2.0 times all the 2023-24 exposure on every line (buildings 47,376 against 23,468; contents 59,016 against 29,058; motor 79,007 against 38,969).
findings.method: Policy rows were joined to non-repudiated claims on policy_id, line and a loss date inside the period. Net cost = incurred_to_date - recoveries. Exposure was recomputed as (end - start + 1)/365. Bodily injury and subsidence were developed with a cost-weighted report-lag pattern from the developed 2021-22 loss years, applied by loss month (factors for 2023/2024: bodily injury 1.07/1.64, subsidence 1.02/1.88). The bootstrap resamples policy rows 2,000 times and does not include development error.
findings.implication: No single market factor works. Motor and contents run below developed cost, and buildings is close to it only because fire is much worse. Frequency and severity need separate adjustments per line and peril; one Part 1 price scaled by a constant would mis-price perils in opposite directions.
findings.adjustment: Carry the Part 1 structure and recalibrate the base level by peril, as frequency x severity, to emerging 2023-24 ultimate experience (findings 2, 3 and 5). As a control, check that predicted 2025 totals per unit of exposure, before the 2025 mix, trend and new-business effects, reconcile to roughly 416 / 89 / 445.

The bodily-injury factors are 1.07/1.64 and subsidence 1.02/1.88. Frequencies: buildings 45.0 against 44.6, excluding fire 42.0 against 42.7, contents 34.3 against 40.5. Motor ultimate frequency is 184.0 against 137.3. Test exposure is 2.0 times training exposure on every line. The problem is the denominator. findings.title: Costs are lower by a near-uniform factor: motor x0.61, buildings excluding fire x0.70, contents x0.79
findings.evidence: Geometric-mean severity, emerging against developed, for the same years (2023-24), adjusted for peril, on claims reported within 90 days: motor 0.612 (95% CI 0.591-0.634), buildings 0.699 (0.642-0.761), contents 0.788 (0.724-0.858). On closed claims, the ratios are flat across the distribution. Motor ratios at the 25th/50th/75th percentiles are 0.65/0.66/0.66 for glass/hail, 0.58/0.64/0.60 for own damage, 0.65/0.63/0.62 for third-party property and 0.63/0.58/0.61 for bodily injury. Sum insured distributions match (buildings median 226k/233k in both markets; contents 35.5k against 39.3k), as do compulsory and voluntary excesses (motor 250/271-275, home 350/~200). findings.method: OLS of log(net) on peril dummies, a 2024 dummy and an emerging dummy, by line, on claims with net > 0 and report lag of 90 days or less, excluding subsidence. Quantile ratios use closed claims from policy years 2023-24 in both markets.
findings.implication: Developed severity relativities (shape) can be carried over, but developed absolute severities overstate emerging cost by 20-40% except for fire. A model fitted on developed data and applied to emerging rows without a severity rebase would over-predict motor most of all.
findings.adjustment: Apply a severity multiplier by line, or preferably by peril, to the carried-over Part 1 severity and pure-premium models: motor 0.61, buildings non-fire 0.70, contents 0.79, with fire handled separately (finding 5). Actual/expected (95% CI) by peril: motor own damage 1.13 (1.09-1.18), third-party property 1.35 (1.30-1.41), bodily injury 1.42 (1.30-1.56), theft 1.36 (1.23-1.50), glass/hail 0.78 (0.74-0.83, see finding 4), all motor 1.18 (1.16-1.21). Buildings: storm 1.26 (1.15-1.38), escape of water 1.09 (0.97-1.23), flood 0.84 (0.68-1.05), subsidence 1.15 (0.87-1.50), fire 1.00 (0.79-1.26), accidental damage 0.87 (0.72-1.03). Contents: theft 1.14 (1.03-1.25), accidental damage 0.85 (0.76-0.94), escape of water 1.16 (1.00-1.35), flood 1.29 (1.05-1.60), all 1.04 (0.98-1.10). Shapes agree on one-way views. Declared prior claims 0/1/2: 1.00/1.24/1.73 against 1.00/1.26/1.53. Flood frequency by flood zone: zone 3 at 6.2 against 6.8 per 1,000, zone 5 at 60 against 74. Subsidence on clay: 3.9 against 3.7. One relativity is weaker in emerging: NCB 0 at 1.73 against 2.56.
findings.method: sklearn PoissonRegressor (alpha 1e-5) on developed 2023-24 rows with exposure weights. Features common to both markets: age band (derived from developed driver_age), NCB band, years-licensed band, cover type, vehicle use, urban density, new business, and linear weather terms for motor; flood zone, soil, property type, urban density, new business and seven weather terms for home. A/E = emerging actual count / predicted count; CI from a Poisson count on A.
findings.implication: The Part 1 relativity structure is transferable on the factors both markets share; what changes is the base frequency per peril. Emerging has about 450-2,700 claims per motor peril, enough for credible peril-level base factors; home perils outside storm, theft and accidental damage have only 50-270 claims, so wide CIs remain.
findings.adjustment: Keep the developed relativities as an offset and refit only peril-level intercepts on emerging data, credibility-weighted towards 1 where the CI includes 1 (buildings flood, subsidence, escape of water; contents escape of water). Consider letting NCB be re-estimated (flatter in emerging). Do not refit full models on 2 years of emerging data.

check.note: The home figures reproduce. The motor figures reproduce only under one weather specification, and the motor base level swings from 1.06 to 1.20 with that choice. Method: sklearn PoissonRegressor (alpha 1e-5) per peril, fitted on developed 2023-24 with exposure weights. Features: age, NCB and years-licensed bands, cover type, vehicle use, urban density and new business, plus standardised weather; for home, flood zone, soil, property type, urban density, new business and seven weather terms. A/E is taken on emerging 2023-24. Home with seven weather terms: storm 1.26 (1.15-1.38), escape of water 1.08, flood 0.83, subsidence 1.14, fire 1.00, accidental damage 0.89; contents theft 1.13, accidental damage 0.84, escape of water 1.18, flood 1.23, all 1.03. All of these agree with the finding to within 0.06. The motor figures match only with four weather terms (hail, wind, freezing, rainfall): bodily injury 1.41, glass/hail 0.78, own damage 1.13, theft 1.34, third-party property 1.35, and a separate all-peril model 1.18. Under that same specification, the per-peril models add up to 1.11. The one-way views all reproduce: 17-24 1.53 against 1.72; 50-64 0.72 in both; third party only 0.48 against 0.44; prior claims 1/2 at 1.24/1.73 against 1.26/1.52; flood zone 3 6.2 against 6.8 and zone 5 59.8 against 74.0; clay subsidence 3.90 against 3.73; NCB 0 1.73 against 2.56. Motor theft has 389 claims, below the stated 450 minimum.
check.corrected_evidence: Motor A/E depends on which weather terms are extrapolated from the developed fit. All seven weather terms: bodily injury 1.56, glass/hail 0.70, own damage 1.09, theft 1.07, third-party property 1.34; the perils sum to 1.06 (95% CI 1.03-1.08), and a single all-peril model gives 1.13. Four weather terms: per-peril sum 1.11, all-peril model 1.18. Hail days only: per-peril sum 1.07. No weather: bodily injury 1.17, glass/hail 1.71, own damage 1.05, theft 1.25, third-party property 1.17, all 1.19-1.20. So the motor base factor is 1.06-1.20, not 'about 1.18'. Bodily injury runs 1.17-1.56 and theft 1.07-1.35. The quoted Poisson CIs cover sampling error only and understate this specification uncertainty. Motor claim counts per peril are 389-2,672.

findings.title: Emerging weather lies largely outside the developed range, and log-linear extrapolation of developed weather terms mis-prices glass/hail
findings.evidence: Mean weather, emerging 2023/2024/2025 against developed 2021-25: wildfire index 0.50/0.55/0.53 against 0.13-0.18; hail days 14.0/17.1/11.4 against 5.6-6.8; rainfall 1,375-1,381 mm against 981-1,144 mm; freezing days 21.0/17.5/28.9 against 35-41. Of emerging motor exposure, 46% has 15 or more hail days, against 4.9% in developed; 57% of emerging buildings exposure has wildfire of 0.5 or more, against 0.16%. Where ranges overlap, the absolute frequencies match. Glass/hail per 1,000 by hail band (<5/5-10/10-15/15-25/25+): developed 13.5/20.6/29.4/37.6/60.3, emerging 14.4/19.0/30.9/41.3/56.1. Yet the developed GLM with a log-linear hail term gives emerging glass/hail A/E 0.78, an over-prediction of about 22%. Escape-of-water frequency is 0.68 times developed on raw figures but A/E 1.09 once freezing days are allowed for (a warmer climate). Applying the emerging band frequencies to the 2025 weather mix of the test rows, against 2023-24, changes expected frequency by: glass/hail x0.83, subsidence x0.84, fire x1.08, escape of water x1.03, storm x0.99.
findings.method: Weather joined on address_id and policy year. Same-band frequency comparisons. The A/E comes from the GLM in finding 3. The 2025 projection reweights the emerging 2023-24 band frequencies by the 2025 test exposure in each band (test rows joined to 2025 weather).
findings.implication: Developed weather effects are roughly right in absolute level but must not be extrapolated exponentially. Tree models from Part 1 would instead cap at the developed edge, under-pricing the extremes (fire at wildfire 0.7 or above, and hail at 25 days or more). Lower 2025 hail and dry-summer values mean glass/hail and subsidence should be priced below the 2023-24 average.
findings.adjustment: For glass/hail, storm, fire, subsidence and escape of water, re-estimate the weather slope on pooled developed and emerging data, linear or splined in the weather index and not exponential beyond the developed range, or fit the emerging slope with the developed slope as a prior. Use the 2025 weather in the test rows. Storm keeps a residual of x1.26 after wind and hail, so it needs an emerging base factor.

check.note: Mostly reproduces; one weather mean is misstated and several 2025 factors depend on the banding. Weather was joined on address_id and year. Weather-table means: wildfire 0.503/0.549/0.528 against 0.132-0.178; hail 13.97/17.08/11.41 against 5.64-6.77; freezing 21.0/17.5/28.9 against 34.7-41.3; developed rainfall 981-1,144. All confirmed. Exposure shares: 46.4% of motor at 15 or more hail days against 4.9%; 57.3% of buildings at wildfire 0.5 or more against 0.16%. Glass/hail per 1,000 by hail band reproduces: developed 2023-24 13.5/20.6/29.4/37.6/60.2, though the 25+ band has only 20 claims; emerging 14.4/19.0/30.9/41.3/56.1. Raw buildings escape-of-water frequency ratio is 0.676. For the 2025 projection, I reweighted emerging 2023-24 band frequencies by 2025 test exposure. Glass/hail x0.82-0.83 holds whatever the bands. The other factors move with the banding. The glass/hail A/E of 0.78 is itself specification-dependent: 0.70 with all seven weather terms, 0.74 with hail only, 1.71 with no weather. That supports the finding's warning about exponential extrapolation.
check.corrected_evidence: Emerging rainfall is 1,381/1,375/1,251 mm for 2023/2024/2025. The 2025 figure is not inside the stated 1,375-1,381, which covers 2023-24 only. 2025 weather-mix factors across alternative bandings: glass/hail x0.82-0.83; subsidence (dry-summer bands) x0.78-0.84; fire (wildfire bands) x1.10-1.12 (stated x1.08); escape of water (freezing-day bands) x1.03-1.09; storm (wind bands) x0.99-1.01.

findings.title: Fire is the main new risk: total losses at sum insured are 4.5 times developed and drive the buildings tail and the 2023-24 swing
findings.evidence: Emerging fire cost per unit of exposure in 2023-24 is 185.3 (90% bootstrap 127-254), against about 100 in developed (94.0 and 104.9 in 2023 and 2024), or x1.86. By year it was 283.4 in 2023 and 93.0 in 2024 (49 claims, then 21). Buildings excluding fire is stable: 231.6 in 2023 and 229.4 in 2024 after development. In 11 of 70 emerging fire claims, cost reached at least 99% of sum insured; they make up 57.6% of fire cost. That is 0.47 total losses per 1,000 exposure, against 0.10 in developed (31 of 586 claims, 26.5% of cost). Emerging claims are capped at sum insured (largest ratio 1.0004); developed claims run up to 1.48 times sum insured. Mean fire severity is 62.1k against 51.7k, the only peril where emerging costs more. Fire frequency is 6.48 per 1,000 at wildfire 0.7 or above (21 claims, 3,242 exposure), against 2.2-2.8 at 0.3-0.7. At wildfire 0.3-0.5, where the two markets overlap, emerging and developed agree: 2.82 against 3.00 per 1,000.
findings.method: Fire claims joined to their row's sum insured (rows with corrected or erroneous sum insured of 10m or more excluded; no emerging claims were affected). Total loss = incurred / sum insured >= 0.99. Wildfire bands use the address's weather for the policy year. Bootstrap of policy rows as in finding 1.
findings.implication: Fire cost depends on sum insured and wildfire, not on repair cost, so the 0.70 cost factor must not be applied to it. With about 22 total losses expected in 2025 (0.47 per 1,000 x 47,376), 2025 buildings cost is volatile: the 2023-24 average is uncertain by roughly +/-35% on its own. A model fitted to 2024 alone would understate fire by about half; one fitted to 2023 alone would overstate it by about half.
findings.adjustment: Model buildings fire separately: total-loss frequency x sum insured (capped at sum insured), driven by wildfire index, plus a partial-loss component at the developed severity shape x about 1.1. Pool both years, use 2025 wildfire, and report a wide range. Cap predicted fire severity at sum insured.

check.note: Reproduced. Emerging fire ultimate cost per unit of exposure, 2023-24: 185.3 (90% bootstrap of policy rows 130-250, stated 127-254). Developed: 94.0/104.9, pooled 99.4, so x1.86. By year 283.4 and 93.0, from 49 and 21 claims. Buildings excluding fire: 231.6 and 229.4. Total losses (incurred/sum insured of 0.99 or more): 11 of 70 emerging fire claims, 57.6% of fire cost, 0.469 per 1,000 exposure. Developed: 31 of 586 (two rows with sum insured of 10m or more excluded), 26.5% of cost, 0.103 per 1,000. Ratio 4.5. Largest claim-to-sum-insured ratio is 1.0004 in emerging against 1.479 in developed. Fire frequency by wildfire band (<0.3/0.3-0.5/0.5-0.7/0.7+): emerging 1.74/2.82/2.16/6.48 per 1,000, with 21 claims on 3,242 exposure at 0.7+. Developed 1.83/3.00 in the bands it reaches. Expected 2025 total losses: 0.469 x 47.376 = 22.2. Single-year bias: 93.0/185.3 = 0.50 and 283.4/185.3 = 1.53. One small discrepancy: developed mean fire severity is 50.2k on the 586 claims (50.7k on all 588), not 51.7k; emerging is 62.1k. That gives x1.24, consistent with the closed-claim mean ratio.

findings.title: Large claims: the motor bodily-injury tail is the developed tail scaled by 0.61; the buildings tail is heavier; contents has none
findings.evidence: Motor bodily injury, 2023-24: developed P(X > t) against emerging P(X > 0.61t), for t = 10k/25k/50k/100k/200k, is 0.495/0.499, 0.190/0.192, 0.060/0.056, 0.019/0.016 and 0.0056/0.0045. The bodily-injury frequency is x1.42, so scaled large-claim frequency is also about x1.4. Emerging excesses over 30.5k number 25: GPD shape 0.37 (bootstrap 90% -0.18 to 0.62), against developed 0.48 over 50k (0.30 without the 11.89m claim). Emerging has 10 claims above 50k (0.26 per 1,000, against 0.50) and a largest claim of 155,655; excess over 50k is 2.5% of motor cost against 10.6%. Developed has 4 of 7,512 bodily-injury claims above 500k and 1 above 10m. With about 1,150 emerging bodily-injury claims expected in 2025, scaling gives roughly 0.6 claims above 305k and about a 14% chance of a claim on the scale of the 11.89m one (around 7m), worth about 14 per unit of motor exposure (about 3% of loss cost). Buildings: emerging P(X > 0.7t) is above developed P(X > t) at every threshold, 1.04% against 0.33% at t = 200k; raw P(X > 100k) is 1.52% against 1.05%. 20 of the 33 emerging buildings claims above 50k are fire. Contents: one claim above 50k (largest 50,885); developed has 15.
findings.method: Empirical exceedance probabilities on bodily-injury and buildings net claim amounts (policy years 2023-24) at the developed threshold and at the threshold x the line severity factor. scipy genpareto fit with floc=0, and a 500-draw bootstrap of the emerging shape.
findings.implication: Two years of emerging data cannot estimate the motor tail and contain no catastrophic bodily-injury claim. Using emerging data alone would understate expected large-claim cost; using developed data unscaled would overstate it. For buildings, scaling the developed 50k large-claim model by 0.7 would understate the fire-driven tail.
findings.adjustment: Motor: carry the Part 1 large-claim GLM and GPD, with the threshold and scale x0.61 (about 30.5k), shape from developed (0.3-0.5, tested as a sensitivity), and large-claim frequency x about 1.4. Buildings: take the large-claim component from the fire total-loss model (finding 5), not scaled down. Contents: no large-claim split.

check.note: Every number reproduces. Two comparisons, though, overstate how far the emerging motor tail is below developed. Bodily-injury exceedance, developed P(X>t) against emerging P(X>0.61t), policy years 2023-24 (3,227 and 449 claims): 0.495/0.499, 0.190/0.192, 0.060/0.056, 0.019/0.016, 0.0056/0.0045. Emerging GPD over 30.5k: 25 excesses, shape 0.37, 500-draw bootstrap 90% -0.17 to 0.65. Emerging motor has 10 claims above 50k (0.257 per 1,000, all bodily injury, largest 155,655) against 198 in developed (0.496). Excess over 50k: 2.5% against 10.6% of motor cost. Developed bodily injury across all loss years: 4 of 7,512 claims above 500k, 1 above 10m. That gives 0.61 expected claims above 305k among 1,150, and P(at least one 11.89m-scale claim) = 1-exp(-1150/7512) = 14%, worth about 14 per unit of exposure. Buildings: emerging P(X>0.7t) is above developed P(X>t) at every threshold, 1.04% against 0.33% at 200k; raw P(X>100k) 1.52% against 1.05%. 20 of the 33 emerging claims above 50k are fire. Contents: 1 claim above 50k (50,885) against 15 developed in 2023-24.

Developed GPD shape over 50k: 2023-24 is 0.50 with the claim and 0.32 without; all years 2021-24 is 0.48 with and 0.42 without. The finding pairs the all-years 0.48 with the 2023-24 0.30. The sensitivity range for the developed shape should be about 0.32-0.50.

findings.title: Reporting and settlement patterns match developed, so the Part 1 development method carries over; 2024 bodily injury and subsidence are about 60% reported
findings.evidence: Loss year 2023 at the same valuation date (2024-12-31), emerging against developed. Bodily-injury mean lag 165 against 152 days, cost reported within 365 days 0.888 against 0.933, open share 0.47 against 0.49. Subsidence mean lag 88 against 124 days (n = 32), open share 0.41 against 0.35. All other perils have at least 97% of cost reported within 90 days in both markets. Open shares by peril and year agree within a few points (for example third-party property 2024: 0.25 against 0.27). With the developed 2021-22 lag pattern: emerging bodily injury 2023/2024 reported 9.10 per 1,000 in 2024, rising to 14.4 ultimate; loss cost 100.2 reported, 164.2 ultimate (2023: 147.9 reported, 158.7 ultimate). Subsidence 2024 rises from 17.8 to 33.5. After development, emerging motor loss cost is flat: 443.4 in 2023, 446.6 in 2024.
findings.method: Report lag = report_date - loss_date, measured for loss year 2023 in both markets. A cost-weighted cumulative reported share F(lag) was estimated from developed loss years 2021-22, which are nearly complete to 730 days. Emerging claims were grossed up by 1/F(age at mid-month).
findings.implication: The apparent 2023-to-2024 fall in emerging motor (433 to 383 reported) and in buildings subsidence is reporting, not experience. The emerging sample is too small (266 bodily-injury claims in 2023) to estimate its own pattern.
findings.adjustment: Apply the Part 1 development (chain ladder by peril; Bornhuetter-Ferguson for 2024 bodily injury and subsidence, with the prior from emerging 2023 loss cost) to the emerging target. Do not estimate development from emerging data. Simple factors used here: bodily injury 2024 x1.64, subsidence 2024 x1.88. Treat development as a stated source of uncertainty: Part 1's backtest found motor bodily injury over-developed by x1.09-1.13.

check.note: Reproduced for loss year 2023 at the 2024-12-31 valuation. Bodily injury: mean lag 164.5 against 151.9 days; cost reported within 365 days 0.888 against 0.933; open share 0.47 against 0.49. Subsidence: n = 32, mean lag 87.6 against 124.4, open share 0.41 against 0.35. Every other peril has at least 97.3% of its cost reported within 90 days in both markets. Open shares in 2024 agree, for example third-party property 0.25 against 0.27 and own damage 0.17 against 0.17. Emerging bodily injury: 2023 rises from 147.9 reported to 158.7 ultimate; 2024 from 100.2 to 164.2, with frequency 9.10 to 14.4 under the count-weighted pattern (14.9 cost-weighted). Subsidence 2024: 17.8 to 33.5. Motor ultimate: 443.4 and 446.6, against reported 432.7 and 382.7. 266 emerging bodily-injury claims in loss year 2023. Caveats: 2024 subsidence is 53% reported (17.8/33.5), not 'about 60%'; bodily injury is 61%. Emerging bodily injury reports slightly slower within 365 days (0.888 against 0.933), but the 90% bootstrap for emerging, 0.81-0.95, includes the developed value. So 'matches developed' is consistent with the data rather than established, and the developed pattern may slightly under-develop emerging 2024 bodily injury.

findings.title: From 2023 to 2024, emerging is stable after development and fire; it cannot support its own trend estimate
findings.evidence: Change in ultimate loss cost from 2023 to 2024: motor +0.7% (443.4 to 446.6), contents -4.7% (91.1 to 86.8), buildings excluding fire -1.0% (231.6 to 229.4), buildings in total -37% (515.0 to 322.4, all from fire). Severity year effect (log-mean, peril-adjusted, claims reported within 90 days), 2024 against 2023, with 95% CI: emerging motor +5.7% (-1.2% to +13.1%), buildings +9.2% (-7.8% to +29.3%), contents +0.4% (-14.5% to +17.9%). Developed, same years: motor +9.8%, buildings +10.3%, contents +5.8%; Part 1 projected trends are +3.8%, +5.3% and +4.2% a year. Short-tail motor frequency fell in both markets: own damage -12% emerging against -3% developed; third-party property -10% against -9%; theft -6% against -6%. Glass/hail rose 16% in emerging as hail days rose from 14.0 to 17.1. Exposure grew about 6% a year on each line.
findings.method: Per-peril frequency by policy year from recomputed exposure. Severity year effects from OLS of log(net) on peril dummies and year dummies, run separately per market. Ultimate figures from finding 7.
findings.implication: One year-on-year step from 1,000-7,000 claims cannot separate trend from noise; every emerging CI includes the developed trend. Carrying no trend would understate 2025 by about 6-8% if emerging inflation matches developed.
findings.adjustment: Project the 2023-24 emerging base to 2025 (1.5 years from the mid-point) with the Part 1 line trends: motor x1.058, buildings x1.081, contents x1.064. Show 0% and 2 x trend as sensitivities. Apply the 2025 weather (finding 4) separately rather than through the trend.

check.note: Reproduced. Ultimate change from 2023 to 2024: motor +0.7%, contents -4.7%, buildings excluding fire -1.0%, buildings total -37.4% (515.0 to 322.4). Severity year effect: OLS of log(net) on peril dummies plus a 2024 dummy, net > 0, lag of 90 days or less, subsidence excluded. Emerging: motor +6.4% (-0.4% to +13.7%; stated +5.7%, -1.2% to +13.1%), buildings +9.2% (-7.8% to +29.3%), contents +0.4% (-14.5% to +17.9%). Developed: motor +9.6%, buildings +10.5%, contents +5.8%. Every emerging CI still includes the developed step and the Part 1 trends. Frequency change by peril: emerging own damage -11.8% against -2.9% developed; third-party property -9.9% against -8.8%; theft -5.7% against -6.2%; glass/hail +16.2% in emerging. Emerging exposure growth +6.0% to +6.6% by line. Trend factors check: 1.038^1.5 = 1.0575, 1.053^1.5 = 1.0805, 1.042^1.5 = 1.0637. Only the emerging motor severity step differs slightly, and the conclusion is unaffected.

findings.title: New business claims more in both markets by similar amounts after mix; with 76% of 2025 rows new business and none with in-house history, this is a material assumption
findings.evidence: New-business/renewal frequency ratio net of mix (A/E against a developed GLM without a new-business term), with 95% CI. Motor: emerging 1.12 (1.03-1.21), developed 1.10 (1.08-1.13). Contents: 1.38 (1.12-1.69) against 1.17 (1.11-1.24). Buildings: 0.94 (0.74-1.18) against 1.07 (1.01-1.14). Raw emerging per 1,000: motor 229 against 177; contents 45.7 against 33.4; buildings 42.5 against 45.2. Emerging new-business claims number 697, 102 and 77. In 2025, 76% of test rows are new business (motor 68,823 of 90,521). None of them appears in training (0 matching policy or customer IDs). 60,769 of the motor new-business rows start on 1 January, with average exposure 0.88-0.92 against 0.46-0.49 for mid-year organic new business in 2023-24. They are younger: 17-24 share 27.8% against 16.1% for 2025 renewals, but similar to organic new business at 29.6%. Declared prior_claims_5y averages 0.264, the same as organic new business (0.268). The channel mix also matches (broker about 70%).
findings.method: As in finding 3, without the new-business feature; A/E split by the new_business flag; ratio CI from Poisson counts on both groups. Test mix compared from the test files joined to customers and addresses.
findings.implication: Applying a developed-strength new-business load to 77% of 2025 exposure, instead of the 8% in training, raises motor about 7%, contents about 12% and buildings about 5% against a training-mix average. Whether a block-transferred broker portfolio behaves like self-selected organic new business cannot be observed. The matching declared claims history and age mix suggest no extra adverse selection, but this is inference. The Part 1 claim-history credibility factor will be neutral (1.0) for all of these rows.
findings.adjustment: Include a new-business factor credibility-weighted between emerging and developed (motor about 1.10, contents about 1.2, buildings about 1.0-1.07). Keep the declared prior_claims_5y relativity, which holds (1.24/1.73 for 1/2 claims). Rebalance the claim-history factor so that rows with no history price at the portfolio mean, not at claim-free renewal level. Report the new-business assumption as a key uncertainty, with a sensitivity of new-business load 1.0 against 1.2.

check.note: The new-business ratios reproduce exactly. One description of the 2025 book is wrong. Buildings: 0.94 (0.74-1.18) against 1.07 (1.01-1.13). Training new-business exposure share: 7.8%. 2025 test: 76.0% of rows are new business (motor 68,823 of 90,521), 76.8-77.0% of exposure. No new-business policy_id or customer_id appears in emerging training. Young drivers (17-24, exposure-weighted): 27.8% against 16.1% for 2025 renewals and 29.6% for organic new business. Declared prior_claims_5y averages 0.264 against 0.268. Broker share is 69.8-70.2%. Average new-business exposure is 0.88-0.92 against 0.46-0.48 in training. The quoted load arithmetic (+7%/+12%/+5%) checks.

findings.title: Recoveries, declined claims and claim-data hygiene work as in Part 1, apart from a small open-claim recovery effect
findings.evidence: Recoveries occur only on closed motor own-damage claims (28-30% recover, at 80% of incurred, which is 23.6-24.5% of own-damage incurred) and closed motor theft claims (12-13% recover, at 30%, which is 3.2-4.6%). Home lines and other motor perils have none. Developed matches: own damage 30-31% at 80%, theft 12-13% at 30%; overall motor recoveries are 5.4% of incurred against 6.0%. Because open claims carry no recovery yet, 2024 own-damage net cost (17% open) is overstated by an implied 5.9% in emerging (5.6% developed), about 1.2% of 2024 motor cost. Declined claims are 120 of 9,258 (1.3%) in emerging against 1.05% in developed. By peril: motor theft 4.4% against 5.0%, third-party property 2.6% against 2.0%, own damage 1.1% against 0.8%, contents theft 1.9% against 2.7%. All have zero incurred and paid, and the declined share does not grow with claim age (developed own damage 2021-24: 0.93/0.80/0.82/0.71%). Emerging has no duplicate claims (developed had 604) and 36 claims outside any policy period (0.39%; 31 with loss dates in 2021-22). Policy exposure has the Part 1 unit error: 492 training rows hold days (x365) or a 360-day year (x1.014), inflating raw buildings 2023 exposure from 11,373 to 18,743. Test exposure is clean (47,376.3 against 47,376.4 recomputed).
findings.method: Recovery rates on closed claims by peril and year. Implied overstatement = open incurred x closed recovery rate / total net. Declined share = repudiated / all claims by loss year. Duplicate check on every field except claim_id. Exposure check: raw against (end - start + 1)/365.
findings.implication: The Part 1 target definition (incurred - recoveries, declined excluded, out-of-period excluded, exposure recomputed) carries over unchanged. Declined claims affect frequency counts only, not cost. Unrecovered open own-damage claims slightly inflate the latest year.
findings.adjustment: Reuse the Part 1 target pipeline as is, without deduplication (no duplicates). Optionally reduce open own-damage incurred by x(1 - 0.24) and open theft by x(1 - 0.04) for expected future recoveries, which lowers motor 2024 by about 1%. No adjustment for declined claims.

Own damage: 28.3%/29.5% recover in 2023/2024, at 80% of incurred, which is 23.6%/24.5% of incurred. Theft: 12.9%/11.7% recover, at 30%, which is 4.6%/3.2%. Developed: own damage 29.5-30.7% recover at 80%; theft 12.0-14.9% at 30%.
