By peril, emerging against developed 2023-24: motor theft 4.4% against 5.0%, third-party property 2.6% against 2.0%, own damage 1.1% against 0.8%, contents theft 1.9% against 2.7%. Developed own-damage declines by loss year 2021-24: 0.93/0.80/0.82/0.71%. Emerging has 0 duplicates against 604 developed. Raw 2023 buildings exposure is 18,743 against 11,373 recomputed. findings.title: Emerging reporting delays match the developed market for every peril, within what the data can test
findings.evidence: Loss year 2023, lags up to 365 days, where both markets are fully observed at 31 Dec 2024. Two-sample KS tests, emerging against developed: bodily injury p=0.51 (n 242 against 1,879; median lag 108 against 104 days), subsidence p=0.44 (32 against 362; median 66.5 against 82.5), third-party property p=0.99 (median 14 against 14), own damage p=0.15 (7 against 7), escape of water p=0.99, storm p=0.95. Truncation-corrected, cost-weighted share of cost reported within 90 days: bodily injury 0.350 in both markets; subsidence 0.524 against 0.489; fast perils 0.967–1.000 against 0.982–0.997. Within 365 days: bodily injury 0.821 against 0.846. Settlement speed by fully observed loss half-year shows no year-on-year change in either market (fast perils: P(lag ≤ 30 | lag ≤ 183) 0.948–0.965 across 2021–2024). Within the emerging market, lag does not vary by region (Kruskal–Wallis on bodily injury across E01–E06, p=0.73; fast-peril mean lag 12.1–13.6 days in every region).
findings.method: Claims cleaned as in Part 1: repudiated excluded, kept only where loss_date falls inside a policy row of the same line (no exact duplicates exist in emerging), net = incurred − recoveries. KS and Mann–Whitney tests on lags of 2023 losses capped at 365 days, the window both markets observe in full. Full patterns from a cost-weighted right-truncation product-limit estimator, F(l) = ∏_{k>l}(1 − d_k/n_k) (Part 1 §3.1), fitted on loss years 2021–24 (developed) and 2023–24 (emerging).
findings.implication: Nothing in the data rejects carrying the Part 1 reporting patterns over. The different climate, customers and regulation have not shown up in reporting speed over the first year after loss.
findings.adjustment: Develop emerging 2023–24 claims with the Part 1 developed patterns by line and peril (sql/10 logic), refitted on the de-duplicated developed claims. Do not fit separate emerging patterns.

check.note: Reproduced from the data. Claims were rebuilt: 604 developed duplicates removed (none in emerging), repudiated claims excluded, loss date inside a policy row of the same line, net = incurred − recoveries. On 2023 losses with lag ≤365: KS p-values are bodily injury 0.510 (n 242 against 1,879; medians 108 against 104), subsidence 0.435 (32 against 362; 66.5 against 82.5), third-party property 0.991, own damage 0.147, escape of water pooled across lines 0.993 (0.32 and 0.38 per line), storm 0.953. Cost-weighted truncation product-limit F(90): bodily injury 0.3495 against 0.3496; subsidence 0.524 against 0.489; fast perils 0.967–1.000 against 0.983–0.997. F(365) for bodily injury: 0.821 against 0.846. Kruskal–Wallis on emerging bodily injury by region: p=0.731. Fast-peril mean lag by region: 12.09–13.57 days. Three minor qualifications. (a) The 0.948–0.965 range for P(lag≤30 | lag≤183) only reproduces when third-party property is excluded (developed 0.949–0.952, emerging 0.947–0.966). With third-party property included it is 0.903–0.914, still flat across half-years, so the conclusion stands. This measures reporting speed, not settlement speed. (b) Contents theft on its own differs slightly (Mann–Whitney p=0.030, KS p=0.14; mean 6.0 against 5.3 days). That is immaterial and expected among roughly 15 tests. (c) The adjustment says to use 'sql/10 logic', but the later findings' numbers use a different estimator (see finding 3).

findings.title: Emerging data cannot identify the reporting tail, so its own patterns carry very little credibility
findings.evidence: No emerging loss is older than 730 days at valuation, so lags beyond about 730 days cannot be observed at all. Developed bodily injury reports 2.55% of its cost after 730 days and 0.86% after 1,000; subsidence 1.44% after 545 days and 0.03% after 730. Bootstrap (300 resamples of claims) of the 2024 bodily injury development factor: developed pattern mean 1.725, sd 0.043 (p5–p95 1.66–1.80); emerging pattern mean 1.801, sd 0.177 (1.53–2.10). Subsidence 2024: developed 1.441, sd 0.032; emerging 1.321, sd 0.116. Inverse-variance credibility on the emerging pattern is about 6% for bodily injury and 7% for subsidence.
findings.method: The product-limit estimator was refitted on each bootstrap resample of each market's slow-peril claims and applied to emerging 2024 claims grouped by loss quarter (factor = 1 / mean F(age) over the days of the quarter). Credibility Z = var_D / (var_D + var_E). This ignores any true difference between the markets, which the data cannot detect.
findings.implication: The tail beyond two years must come from Part 1. It is an assumption that emerging data cannot test, and it is the one most exposed to the different regulation (limitation periods drive bodily injury tails).
findings.adjustment: Use the developed tail beyond 365 days for every peril. If any blending is wanted, weight the emerging pattern at about 5–10% on bodily injury and subsidence only. State the >730-day tail (2.55% of bodily injury cost) as an untested carry-over assumption.

check.note: Maximum emerging age at valuation is 730 days. Developed bodily injury cost F(730)=0.9745 and F(1000)=0.9914, so 2.55% and 0.86% of cost report after those lags. Subsidence F(545)=0.9856 and F(730)=0.9997, so 1.44% and 0.03%. I re-ran the bootstrap: 300 claim resamples, product-limit refitted each time, applied to emerging 2024 claims by loss quarter with factor = reported / mean F over the quarter's days. Bodily injury: developed mean 1.724, sd 0.045 (p5–p95 1.67–1.81); emerging 1.799, sd 0.183 (1.56–2.15). Subsidence: developed 1.441, sd 0.031; emerging 1.316, sd 0.110. Credibility Z_emerging is 5.7% for bodily injury and 7.6% for subsidence. All figures are within bootstrap noise of those claimed. The standard deviations are similar under sql/10's claim-weighted estimator (bodily injury 0.034 against 0.174).

findings.title: As-at 31 Dec 2023 against 31 Dec 2024 backtest on emerging 2023: the carried-over pattern works, the emerging-only pattern over-develops
findings.evidence: Cost basis, developed / actual. Developed pattern known at 31 Dec 2023, applied to emerging 2023: buildings 1.021, contents 1.014, motor 0.988; fast perils 1.000–1.014; bodily injury 0.948; subsidence 1.238 (0.35m reported, 32 claims). Emerging pattern alone (one loss year, lags up to 364 days): buildings 0.996, contents 1.007, motor 1.050, bodily injury 1.129. Count basis: developed pattern gives bodily injury 1.039 and subsidence 1.162, fast perils 0.94–1.04 (the extremes are the smallest perils); the emerging pattern gives bodily injury 1.178. Reference run on developed 2023 with the same code: bodily injury cost 1.328 against raw actual (reproduces Part 1's 1.326), 1.201 excluding the 11.9m claim, but 1.008 on counts. Share reported at 31 Dec 2023 by count is the same in both markets (bodily injury 0.570 emerging, 0.567 developed). By cost it is not (0.447 against 0.570 ex-large claim), because emerging bodily injury claims reported in 2023 averaged 8.4k against 10.5k for the full year.
findings.method: Each market was rebuilt from report_date ≤ 2023-12-31. Patterns were estimated at that date (developed loss years 2021–23; emerging 2023 only) and the 2023 loss year developed by quarter. 'Actual' is 2023 as known at 31 Dec 2024, grossed up for the remaining tail with the current developed pattern (bodily injury ×1.078); ratios against the raw actual are also shown. Current incurred values are used throughout because the data is a single snapshot.
findings.implication: The test supports carrying patterns over and rejects emerging-only patterns. Its limits: it tests reporting (IBNR) only, not movement in case estimates; the 2023 actual still carries an untested tail; and 161 bodily injury claims at the earlier date give a binomial standard error of about 5% on the ratio. Cost-weighted chain ladder on bodily injury errs by −5% to +33% across the two markets, while counts err by +1% to +4%.
findings.adjustment: Report this backtest as the evidence for the carry-over. For bodily injury, develop counts (claim numbers) with the developed pattern and handle cost through a severity assumption or BF rather than a cost-weighted chain ladder.

check.note: I rebuilt both markets from report_date ≤ 2023-12-31. Patterns: developed loss years 2021–23, emerging 2023 only. Each pattern was applied to loss-year 2023 quarters. 'Actual' is the current 2023 position grossed up with the current developed pattern (bodily injury ×1.078). Every headline ratio reproduces, but the conclusion that the backtest 'rejects emerging-only patterns' holds only for motor. The emerging-only pattern came closer on buildings, contents and subsidence.
check.corrected_evidence: Developed pattern / actual, cost basis: buildings 1.021, contents 1.013, motor 0.988, bodily injury 0.948, subsidence 1.238. Emerging-only pattern: buildings 0.996, contents 1.006, motor 1.050, bodily injury 1.129, subsidence 1.038. So the developed pattern wins on motor and bodily injury, and the emerging pattern wins on buildings, contents and subsidence. Subsidence rests on 22 claims (0.35m) reported at 31 Dec 2023, not 32. Fast perils pooled by line give 0.999–1.013. By peril the range is 0.887 (buildings storm) to 1.031 (buildings flood). Count basis: bodily injury 1.039 (developed pattern) against 1.178 (emerging pattern); subsidence 1.162; fast perils 0.937–1.041. Developed reference: bodily injury 1.328 against the raw actual and 1.244 against the grossed-up actual; counts 1.008. Excluding the 11.9m claim and refitting the pattern I get 1.187 against the raw actual, not 1.201; without the refit it is 1.289. Against the grossed-up actual it is −5% to +24%; against the raw actual, +2% to +33%. The grossed-up 'actual' uses the developed pattern for the tail, which slightly favours that pattern.

findings.title: The immature 2024 year reverses the sign of the motor trend: reported −12%, developed +3% to +7%
findings.evidence: Emerging reported net across 2023–24 is 28.00m. Developed with the developed pattern it is 30.19m, so IBNR is 2.19m (7.3% of ultimate). Development factors for 2024 (2023): buildings 1.048 (1.004), contents 1.030 (1.002), motor 1.224 (1.028). Bodily injury carries 1.45m of the 1.73m motor 2024 IBNR (84%), at a factor of 1.72. Motor cost per vehicle-year is 432.7 reported in 2023 and 382.7 in 2024 (ratio 0.884). After development the ratio becomes 1.054 (chain ladder, developed pattern), 1.070 (emerging pattern), 1.041 (BF on bodily injury and subsidence) or 1.031 (BF less future recoveries). Contents 0.95 reported, 0.98 developed.
findings.method: Quarter-averaged product-limit factors applied by line, peril and loss quarter. Exposure recomputed as (period_end − period_start + 1)/365, because the emerging raw exposure repeats the Part 1 days/360 issue (about 0.5% of rows, inflating raw exposure by about 40%). BF prior = 2023 developed cost per exposure × 2024 exposure, no trend.
findings.implication: Training on 2024 as reported would understate motor by about 18% and give a false downward trend. With only two years, any error e in 2024's development becomes about 2e in 2025 if the trend is fitted from 2023→2024 and extrapolated.
findings.adjustment: Train on developed targets. Do not estimate the emerging trend from two points: take severity inflation from Part 1 or external data (developed and emerging motor fast-peril gross severity rose 3.7% and 3.1% in 2023→24). Consider giving 2023 at least equal weight with 2024 for motor, because it is 97% developed.

check.note: Reproduced exactly with the estimator the finding describes: ultimate per quarter = reported / mean F(age) over the quarter's days. Reported 2023–24 is 28.00m, developed 30.19m, IBNR 2.19m (7.25%). Factors for 2024 (2023): buildings 1.047 (1.004), contents 1.030 (1.002), motor 1.224 (1.028). Bodily injury factor is 1.721, with IBNR of 1.45m out of a motor 2024 IBNR of 1.72m (84%). Exposure is recomputed with (end − start + 1)/365; the raw values were wrong on 0.36–0.55% of rows and inflate raw exposure by 24–65%, 39–41% for motor. Motor cost per vehicle-year is 432.7 and 382.7 (ratio 0.884). Developed ratios: 1.054, 1.070 with the emerging pattern, 1.041 with BF on bodily injury, 1.030 net of future recoveries. Contents ratio is 0.95 reported and 0.98 developed. Gross fast-peril severity rose 3.65% (developed) and 3.12% (emerging). Important caveat: this is not the sql/10 estimator. sql/10 averages 1/F(age_i) over reported claims weighted by cost, which is a Horvitz–Thompson estimator. Under sql/10 the factors are motor 2024 1.192 and bodily injury 1.626, IBNR is 1.98m (6.6%), and the motor ratio is 1.026 by chain ladder and about 1.02 with BF. The sign reversal holds either way, but the team must pick one estimator. The choice moves 2024 motor by 0.25m (2.7%).

findings.title: For 2024 bodily injury use BF or frequency × severity; the chain ladder implies an implausible severity jump
findings.evidence: 2024 bodily injury: reported 2.01m (183 claims, 58.1% of estimated ultimate cost), which triggers Part 1's BF rule (< 75% reported). Estimates: chain ladder with the developed pattern 3.47m; with the emerging pattern 3.62m; BF with the 2023 prior 3.36m (3.43m with a 5% trend); count-developed 293.4 claims × 2023 ultimate severity 10.65k × 1.00–1.035 = 3.13–3.24m. Count-developed frequency is stable: 14.97 per 1,000 vehicle-years in 2023, 14.59 in 2024. The chain ladder therefore implies ultimate severity +11% (10.65k to 11.82k), against +3.1% gross severity on emerging motor fast perils. 2024 subsidence: chain ladder 0.31m, BF 0.39m (20 reported claims; developed count frequency 2.88 then 2.54 per 1,000).
findings.method: Chain ladder as in finding 4. Count development uses a count-weighted product-limit pattern. BF = reported + (1 − 1/LDF) × prior. Severity trend from the ratio of 2024 to 2023 average gross incurred on motor non-bodily-injury perils.
findings.implication: Bodily injury makes up about 36% of emerging motor developed cost, so the choice of method moves 2024 motor by up to 0.5m (about 5%) and hence the motor level.
findings.adjustment: Apply Part 1's D-17 BF to emerging 2024 bodily injury and subsidence, using the emerging 2023 developed burning cost as prior (not the developed-market one). Cross-check with frequency × severity. Central estimate for 2024 bodily injury about 3.3–3.4m; carry the 3.1–3.6m range into the uncertainty statement.

check.note: Reproduced with the days-averaged estimator from finding 3. Bodily injury 2024: reported 2.015m on 183 claims, 58.1% of ultimate. Chain ladder 3.468m with the developed pattern and 3.615m with the emerging pattern. BF with the 2023 prior is 3.358m (3.425m with 5% trend); the prior is emerging 2023 ultimate per vehicle-year × 2024 exposure, and 2023 is 92.8% reported, so it qualifies under Part 1's ≥90% rule. Count-developed: 282.4 claims in 2023 and 293.4 in 2024, a frequency of 14.97 and 14.59 per 1,000. The 2023 severity is 10,652, giving frequency × severity of 3.125–3.234m. The chain-ladder severity is 11,820 (+11%). Subsidence 2024: chain ladder 0.310m, BF 0.386m, 20 claims, frequency 2.88 and then 2.54 per 1,000. Bodily injury is 36.4% of developed motor cost, and the method range of 0.49m is 5.2% of 2024 motor. Caveat: under sql/10's claim-weighted estimator the 2024 bodily injury share is 61.5%, which still triggers BF. The chain ladder then gives 3.28m, BF 3.25m and frequency × severity 3.05–3.16m, and the implied severity jump is +7.4%, not +11%. The finding's argument is weaker under the estimator Part 1 actually used. Subsidence frequency × severity on a 2023 severity of 16.0k gives 0.49–0.51m, above both the chain ladder and BF. That spread should go into the uncertainty range.

findings.title: Settlement speed and open shares by age match the developed market; no sign of case under-reserving on fast perils
findings.evidence: Open share by age band since loss, emerging against developed. Motor fast perils: 0–90 days 54.0% against 52.5%; 91–181 days 16.4% against 17.5%; 182–272 days 4.1% against 5.2%. Paid / incurred on open bodily injury claims: 0.214 and 0.157 (2023, 2024) against 0.178 and 0.165. Average incurred per claim by loss quarter does not fall as the open share rises: emerging motor fast 1,635 (2023 Q1, 0% open) to 1,877 (2024 Q4, 53% open), and developed the same. Open bodily injury claims average 11.5–11.6k against 9.4–9.6k closed in both emerging years.

findings.implication: A single snapshot cannot show IBNER directly, but nothing suggests emerging case estimates behave differently from the developed market. The Part 1 decision D-28 (no IBNER uplift on bodily injury) can carry over.
findings.adjustment: None for fast perils. No IBNER uplift on bodily injury, following Part 1 D-28. Flag it as untestable without a second valuation.

check.note: Every number reproduces, but the statement that nothing suggests different case behaviour leaves out a visible difference in bodily injury.
check.corrected_evidence: Open share by 91-day age band, motor fast perils: 54.0/52.5%, 16.4/17.5%, 4.1/5.2%. Buildings fast perils: 62.2/64.7%, 25.4/23.3%. Bodily injury at 364–454 days 56.5/60.5%, and at 637–727 days 35.0/36.1%. Paid/incurred on open bodily injury: 0.214 and 0.157 in emerging against 0.178 and 0.165 in developed. But it means 2024 emerging bodily injury (74% open) could fall back. Treat it as a one-sided downside risk on the bodily injury ultimate, not as 'same as developed'.

findings.title: Recoveries are booked only at closure, which overstates net cost on open motor own-damage and theft claims
findings.evidence: Closed motor own damage: 28.8% of emerging claims carry a recovery, worth 24.0% of incurred (developed 30.1% and 23.6%). Theft: 12.4% and 3.93% (developed 13.1% and 4.00%). No open claim in either market has a recovery, and home lines have none. On net, 2024 Q4 own-damage severity runs 1.174 (emerging) and 1.190 (developed) above the 2023 seasonal pattern; on gross incurred the figures are 0.981 and 1.058, so the apparent excess is missing recoveries. Expected future recoveries on open emerging motor claims are 97k for 2024 (1.26% of 2024 motor reported net) and 0.2k for 2023; developed 1.36m (1.50%).
findings.method: Recovery rate by peril on closed claims, applied to open-claim incurred. The 2024 Q4 / Q1–Q3 severity ratio was divided by the same ratio for 2023 to remove seasonality, on both net and gross.
findings.implication: Without adjustment, the 2024 motor target carries about 1.3% of net cost that will be recovered, which slightly inflates both the level and the apparent 2023→24 motor trend.
findings.adjustment: For open motor own-damage and theft claims, set net = incurred × (1 − closed-claim recovery rate by peril): about 0.76 for own damage and 0.96 for theft. Check whether Part 1 made this adjustment; it is not listed in §2.2.

check.note: Closed own damage: 28.84% of emerging claims carry a recovery, worth 23.99% of incurred, against 30.06% and 23.59% in developed. Theft: 12.36% and 3.93% against 13.14% and 4.00%. findings.title: About 0.4% of fast-peril claims report 13–19 months after loss, none of which is visible yet for 2024
findings.evidence: Developed losses of 2021–22, fast perils: 3 claims at 180–240 days, almost none at 240–390, then 320 at 390–570 days (bins 22/62/70/79/65/18). The 34 emerging claims dated 2021–22 on policies first written in 2023 (net 89.9k, mean lag 464–501 days) fit the same mechanism and are excluded as outside any period. findings.title: New business and broker mix make no material difference to reporting, and the 2025 target is ultimate
findings.evidence: Fast-peril mean lag (lags up to 365): new business 14.1 days against renewal 12.5 in emerging (Mann–Whitney p=0.08); 12.8 against 12.4 in developed (p=0.004). Broker, direct and comparison-site fast-peril mean lags are 11.7–14.7 days. Training new-business share is 12–15%, against 76% in the 2025 test.
findings.method: Claims joined to their policy row; lags compared by new_business flag and channel for 2021–23 losses.
findings.implication: The broker transfer changes risk mix, not development. Because the target is 2025 ultimate cost, how fast 2025 claims report does not enter the prediction, and the new-business share of the training claims is too small to bias the developed targets.
findings.adjustment: None.

check.note: Fast perils, lags ≤365: emerging 2023 losses, new business 14.12 days (n 360) against renewal 12.51 (n 3,898), Mann–Whitney p=0.081. With 2023–24 losses it is 13.28 against 12.18, p=0.032, so it is significant but about one day. Developed 2021–23: 12.77 against 12.40, p=0.0045. Share within 90 days is 0.995–1.000. findings.title: Emerging cost levels differ, so Part 1's BF priors and caps cannot be transplanted
findings.evidence: Average net per claim, emerging against developed. Bodily injury 9.4–11.6k against 17.3–22.7k (by status and year); subsidence 10.4–17.0k against 22.3–28.4k; motor fast 1.5–1.9k against 2.4–3.0k; contents 2.0–3.0k against 2.6–3.1k. Fire is the exception: 66.6–67.7k closed against 51–58k. Emerging has no claim above 1m (largest motor 156k, largest buildings 361k), so the 1m cap in Part 1's BF prior has no effect. Emerging motor fast-peril frequency is about 165–178 per 1,000 vehicle-years against 124–137.
findings.method: Average net per claim by peril, loss year and status; maximum claim size; quarterly frequency as in finding 8.
findings.implication: Reporting patterns carry over, but cost levels do not. Any BF prior, large-claim threshold or capping rule must be rebuilt on emerging data, or the developed-market cost per exposure will roughly double emerging slow-peril IBNR.
findings.adjustment: BF priors from emerging 2023 developed burning cost. If a cap or large-claim split is used, set it from emerging severities: for example, rescale the 1m cap by the emerging/developed bodily injury severity ratio of about 0.5, or use an emerging percentile.

check.note: The severity comparisons hold, but the claim that a developed-market prior would 'roughly double' emerging slow-peril IBNR is overstated. Emerging has higher frequency and lower severity, so its burning cost is not half the developed one.
check.corrected_evidence: Average net per claim, 2023–24 by year and status: emerging bodily injury 9.4–11.6k against developed 17.3–18.0k, or up to 29.0k for 2023 open claims because of the 11.89m claim (17.8–23.3k by loss year 2021–24). Subsidence 10.4–17.0k against 22.3–28.4k. Emerging motor fast perils 1.5–1.9k by loss quarter against 2.6–3.0k. Fire closed claims 66.6–67.7k against 51.1–58.4k. findings.title: The 2023→24 fall in buildings is fire frequency, not immaturity, and with about 1,000 claims a year process risk outweighs development risk
findings.evidence: Emerging buildings cost per exposure: 516.2 in 2023 and 321.3 in 2024 (ratio 0.62–0.64 under every development method). Fire went from 49 claims (4.31 per 1,000) and 3.22m reported in 2023 to 21 claims (1.74 per 1,000) and 1.13m in 2024. Fire reports within a mean of 5.6 days and its 2024 factor is 1.005–1.015. Claims of 100k or more were 39.5% of emerging buildings 2023 cost against 17–20% in the developed market.
findings.method: Developed cost by line, peril and year divided by recomputed exposure; large-claim shares by line and year.
findings.implication: The level and trend for buildings must not be read off 2023→24. The volatility is frequency and severity process variance in a small book, which development cannot fix.
findings.adjustment: For buildings fire and other large-claim perils, borrow the frequency of large claims from Part 1 relativities or pool 2023–24, rather than trending.

check.note: The level figures and the attribution to fire reproduce. The title's volume is wrong, and so is the description of the fire drop as process variance.
check.corrected_evidence: Buildings developed cost per exposure is 516.2 (2023) and 321.2 (2024). The ratio is 0.622 with the developed pattern, 0.621 with the emerging pattern, 0.631 with sql/10's claim-weighted estimator and 0.635 with BF on subsidence; it is 0.596 reported. Fire: 49 claims (4.31 per 1,000) and 3.22m in 2023; 21 claims (1.74 per 1,000) and 1.13m in 2024. Mean lag is 5.6 days, and the 2024 factor is 1.006–1.017. Fire is about 92% of the per-exposure fall in reported buildings cost (−190 of −208); the rest is mostly immature subsidence. Claims ≥100k are 39.5% of emerging 2023 buildings cost against 17.0–19.9% in developed 2021–24. Corrections: buildings has about 520–540 claims a year (the 1,000 is buildings plus contents). The fire frequency fall is not Poisson noise: given 70 claims and the exposure split, P(≤21 in 2024) = 0.0002 (two-sided binomial p = 0.0003). The fall is spread across all months, not one event. It is concentrated in E02 (18 → 2 on about 2,100 exposure) and E06 (13 → 7). Something specific changed, whether regional climate or weather, mix, or a 2023 regional cluster. It should be investigated, for example against the weather table, before choosing between pooling and Part 1 relativities. The recommendation not to trend 2023→24 still stands.

findings.title: Quantified development uncertainty for the uncertainty statement
findings.evidence: 2024 motor developed is about 9.2–9.6m across methods. Components, as one standard deviation: process variance on about 110 unreported bodily injury claims (293.4 − 183), severity 11.2k with CV 1.6, compound Poisson, about 0.22m; pattern parameter (developed-pattern bootstrap) 0.09m; method spread (3.13–3.62m read as ±2 sd) 0.12m; the untested >730-day tail (2.55% of bodily injury cost, ±50%) 0.04m. Combined about 0.27m, or 2.9% of 2024 motor. 2024 buildings and contents IBNR (+4.8% and +3.0%) is dominated by process variance. Total IBNR on 2023–24 is 2.19m, 7.3% of 30.19m.
findings.method: Square root of the sum of squared components. Severity mean and CV from emerging bodily injury claims reported after 180 days. Pattern sd from the bootstrap in finding 2.
findings.implication: Development adds about ±3% (1 sd) to the motor training level, rising to about ±6% if the 2025 trend is extrapolated from 2023→24, and well under ±1% for home lines. It is second-order next to the shift to 76% new business and the cost-level differences, but it is not negligible for motor.
findings.adjustment: Carry ±3% on motor and ±1% on home lines from development into the stated 2025 ranges, and name bodily injury tail carry-over and method choice as the drivers.

check.note: The motor arithmetic reproduces. The comparisons with home lines and with the training level are wrong.
check.corrected_evidence: Motor 2024 developed is 9.17–9.55m across methods, including 9.17m under sql/10's estimator. Components: compound Poisson on 110.4 unreported bodily injury claims, severity 11,173 and CV 1.60 (116 emerging bodily injury claims with lag >180), gives 0.222m. Pattern 0.043 × 2.01m = 0.087m. Method spread (3.13–3.62)/4 = 0.12m. Tail 2.55% × 3.4m × 50% = 0.04m. Combined 0.27m, 2.9% of 2024 motor. That is about 1.5% of the pooled 2023–24 motor training level (17.8m), not ±3%. On the same compound-Poisson basis, process variance on unreported 2024 home claims is 93k for buildings (2.4% of 3.89m, driven by subsidence and fire) and 18.5k for contents (1.4% of 1.34m). The statement 'well under ±1% for home lines' is therefore wrong for 2024. On the pooled 2023–24 level these are about 1.0% and 0.7%. Buildings also carries a subsidence method spread: chain ladder 0.31m, BF 0.39m, frequency × severity 0.49m, up to about 4.6% of buildings 2024. The choice between the days-averaged and sql/10 claim-weighted estimators moves 2024 motor by 0.25m, about one standard deviation. It belongs in the method component. Suggested statement: development adds about ±3% to 2024 motor (±1.5% pooled) and ±1.5–2.5% to 2024 home lines (±1% pooled). Name the estimator choice, the bodily injury tail carry-over and the subsidence method as the drivers.

findings.title: The emerging climate differs sharply from developed, and wildfire and hail run beyond the developed range
findings.evidence: Means over all address-years, emerging 2023-24 against developed 2021-24: rainfall 1,378 vs 1,046 mm (+32%); dry summer index 0.70 vs 0.53; freezing days 19.3 vs 38.1 (-49%); hail days 15.5 vs 6.3 (x2.5); wildfire index 0.53 vs 0.15 (x3.4); temperature 15.5 vs 12.7 C; wind 5.05 vs 4.46. Developed wildfire never exceeds 0.669, yet 21% / 13% / 21% of emerging address-years in 2023 / 2024 / 2025 are above that, and 53-83% are above the developed 99th percentile (0.461). Hail tops out at 83 days against 48 in developed. 23% (2023), 37% (2024) and 10% (2025) of address-years are above the developed 99th percentile of 18 days. Rainfall is above the developed 99th percentile (1,774 mm) on 4-8%. No weather values are missing, every policy and test row joins to weather, and no index is censored at its cap (wildfire = 1.0 on at most 0.02%).
findings.method: DuckDB over emerging/weather.parquet and weather.parquet: means and quantiles by market and year, plus the share of emerging address-years above the developed maximum and 99th percentile.
findings.implication: Any Part 1 relativity on wildfire or hail is applied outside the data it was fitted on. Tree models such as the Part 1 buildings XGBoost hold the prediction flat beyond the last split. Splines and log-linear terms keep extrapolating. Which one is used changes the 2025 prediction for 10-21% of rows.
findings.adjustment: Fit wildfire and hail as explicit parametric terms (wildfire log-linear, hail on log(hail+1), see the hail finding), never as tree splits or clamped splines. Flag the rows beyond developed support and report a sensitivity on them.

check.note: All seven means reproduce (DuckDB, all address-years): rain 1,378 vs 1,046 mm, DSI 0.695 vs 0.526, freezing 19.3 vs 38.1, hail 15.5 vs 6.3 (x2.45), wildfire 0.526 vs 0.153 (x3.4), temp 15.5 vs 12.7, wind 5.05 vs 4.46. No nulls, every train and test row joins to weather, wildfire=1.0 on 0.0075%. The problem is the reference. The developed max 0.669, the p99 0.461 and the hail p99 of 18 all come from the developed weather table INCLUDING 2025, the test year. Part 1 was fitted on 2021-24, so the comparison should use that range. The stated shares reproduce exactly against 2021-25, but not against the fitted range.
check.corrected_evidence: Against Part 1's training support (developed 2021-24): wildfire max 0.635, p99 0.443. Emerging address-years above the max: 23.3% / 18.5% / 22.2% (2023/24/25). Above p99: 55.5% / 88.6% / 70.1%. Hail p99 19 days: 20.8% / 33.2% / 7.8% above. Hail max 48 days, emerging 83, but 0% of 2025 address-years exceed 48: the hail issue is a sparse tail (developed has 78 motor exposure-years at 30+), not strict extrapolation. Rain p99 is 1,787 mm (2021-24) or 1,774 mm (2021-25); 4-8% above either way. The figures as stated (21/13/21% above 0.669; 53/83/63% above 0.461; 23/37/10% above 18) are correct only if the developed 2025 test-year weather is counted as support.

findings.title: Address features match developed; the known data issues recur, construction codes are renamed and missingness has risen
findings.evidence: Flood-zone shares 1/2/3/4/5/missing: emerging 68.6/14.7/7.7/4.3/1.7/3.0% vs developed 68.5/14.7/7.9/4.6/1.4/2.9%. Distance to river p10/p50/p90: 0.42/2.37/6.87 vs 0.42/2.37/6.88 km. Elevation median 7.4-7.6 m in every E region, max 60.0 in all six, so there is no R11-style feet error. Year built p10/p50/p90 1894/1964/2013 in both, and the 1900 placeholder recurs: 4,421 addresses at 1900 against about 420 at each neighbouring year (10.5x; 3.2% of addresses vs 3.3% in developed). Construction codes are now BRK/WOD/MIX/STN, with exposure shares 0.699/0.121/0.102/0.078 against developed brick/timber/non_standard/stone at 0.700/0.121/0.100/0.080. MIX has the highest storm (34.6 per 1,000) and escape-of-water (17.5) frequency, as non_standard does in developed (17.3 and 22.4). Soil type is missing on 12.0% of addresses (developed 2.5%), and river distance on 12.0% (2.5%). Flood zone is missing on 3.0%, unchanged. 2025 test geography matches training: region shares within 0.4 points, flood zone 3+ 13.6% vs 13.7%, clay 31.0% vs 30.6%, soil missing 12.2% vs 12.0%, and new business looks like renewals. 77% of 2025 buildings test addresses never appear in training.
findings.method: Distributions and quantiles by market over addresses.parquet. Developed elevation was checked by region (R11 divided by 3.28 when comparing). Construction shares are exposure-weighted over developed 2023-24 (timber t/w merged). Train vs test mix is exposure-weighted over test files joined to addresses.
findings.implication: The broker portfolio does not shift the geography, so geography is not a source of 2025 mix change. Most 2025 addresses have no history, so location rating must come from address and weather features. Part 1 data fixes apply, except the R11 conversion. Construction must be mapped, or a carried-over model will see unknown levels. The 1900 mapping is inferred from matching shares and relativity order, not from a data dictionary.
findings.adjustment: Map BRK to brick, WOD to timber, MIX to non_standard and STN to stone. Apply the Part 1 year_built = 1900 fix (D-27). Do not convert elevation. Handle the 12% missing soil and river distance as set out in the missingness finding.

check.note: Re-derived from both addresses tables and exposure-weighted policy and test rows. Flood-zone shares 68.6/14.7/7.7/4.3/1.7 and 2.95% missing, vs 68.5/14.7/7.9/4.6/1.4 and 2.92%. River p10/50/90 0.42/2.37/6.87 vs 6.88. Median elevation 7.4-7.6 m and max 60.0 in every E region; developed R11 is 24.6/196.9, so the R11 fix is not needed. year_built=1900 on 4,421 addresses vs 389-426 at neighbouring years (3.23% vs 3.30%). Construction exposure shares BRK/WOD/MIX/STN 0.699/0.121/0.102/0.078 vs 0.700/0.121/0.100/0.080. MIX storm 34.6 and EoW 17.5 per 1,000 (highest), vs developed non_standard 17.3/22.4 in 2023-24. Soil missing 12.04% vs 2.50%; river missing 11.99% vs 2.50%. Test vs train (buildings): regions within 0.4 pts, clay 31.0 vs 30.6, soil missing 12.2 vs 12.0. 77.2% of test exposure (76.9% of rows) is at addresses not in training; new business and renewals have the same geography. Trivial deviations only: developed median year built is 1965 (not 1964); flood zone missing rounds to 2.9%; buildings test zone 3+ is 13.5% (not 13.6%) vs 13.7% train. The BRK/WOD/MIX/STN mapping is an inference, as the finding says.

findings.title: Missing soil and river distance look random in emerging, so the developed missing-value levels should not be applied to 12% of rows
findings.evidence: Soil missing and river missing occur together on 2,031 addresses, against 1,971 expected under independence. The soil missing rate is flat across regions (11.6-12.5%) while the clay share ranges from 11.9% (E01) to 52.5% (E06). In developed, the soil-missing subsidence relativity (x1.66 against non-clay at a dry summer index of 0.6) matches a random mix with a 41.6% clay share: 0.416 x 2.73 + 0.584 = 1.72. Using emerging regional clay shares, the same mix implies x1.21 (E01) to x1.91 (E06). Missing river distance carries no flood signal in emerging: within flood zone 3+ or missing, 18.1 per 1,000 vs 17.5 for known distance. Developed's x1.21 (23.3 vs 19.3, 56 claims) is noise.
findings.method: Cross-tabulation of missingness, the regional soil mix, a Poisson GLM of subsidence on clay, missing soil, dry summer index and clay x index with year effects, and flood frequency by river-missing within flood-zone groups.
findings.implication: A developed missing-value level, or the XGBoost default direction, learnt on 2.5% of rows would now apply to about 12% of emerging rows with a single average. That misprices subsidence for missing-soil rows by up to about 30% depending on region.
findings.adjustment: For missing soil, use the probability-weighted relativity P(clay | region) x clay effect (including clay x dry summer) plus (1 - P) x non-clay. For missing river distance, impute from flood zone and elevation, or set the river term to neutral within the zone. Keep missing flood zone as its own level (see the flood finding).

check.note: The soil half holds. Soil and river missing together: 2,031 addresses vs 1,977 expected (not 1,971). Soil missing is 11.6-12.5% in every region. Clay share of known soil runs from 11.9% (E01) to 52.5% (E06). Developed Poisson GLM (clay, missing soil, DSI-0.6, clay x DSI, year effects): missing-soil x1.656 (log se 0.19, 95% CI about 1.14-2.40), clay x2.73 at 0.6, clay share 41.6%, so the mix is 1.72. Emerging regional mixes are 1.21-1.91. The river half is overstated: the emerging figure rests on 8 claims.
check.corrected_evidence: Within flood zone 3+ or missing, buildings flood is 18.06 per 1,000 with river distance missing vs 17.45 with it known, but only 8 vs 60 claims. Zone-adjusted Poisson relativity: x1.07, 95% CI 0.51-2.24, so the developed effect cannot be ruled out. Contents runs the other way: 12.8 vs 15.4 per 1,000 (7 claims). Developed buildings: 23.3 vs 19.3 (56 claims); zone-adjusted x1.25, CI 0.96-1.63, p=0.10. That is not significant, but not shown to be noise either. Effect of a single 1.66 on missing-soil rows: E01 overpriced by 37% (1.66/1.21), E06 underpriced by 13% (1.66/1.91).

findings.title: Flood: zone, elevation and river relativities carry over at a comparable level; rainfall adds nothing
findings.evidence: Poisson GLM with zone categories and rainfall: a test that the zone and rain slopes are equal across markets gives LR p = 0.29 (buildings) and 0.37 (contents). Missing zone: x56 vs x39 (buildings) and x35.4 vs x35.3 (contents). Within zone 3+ or missing: elevation under 3 m gives 26.1 vs 29.6 per 1,000 and 3-8 m gives 5.2 vs 5.2; river under 0.5 km gives 25.7 vs 29.5 and 0.5-2 km gives 11.0 vs 10.6 (emerging vs developed). Level: developed zone rates applied to emerging exposure expect 92.5 buildings and 81.5 contents flood claims; 80 and 86 were observed (A/E 0.87 and 1.06) despite 32% more rain. Out-of-time test (fit one emerging year, score the other on Poisson deviance with the level matched; 2024 / 2023 gain against intercept only): developed zone relativities held fixed give +127.9 / +95.0 (buildings) and +75.2 / +166.2 (contents). Adding an emerging rainfall slope gives +0.0 / +0.4 and -3.0 / -2.1, and region factors -4.2 / -8.2. In developed, frequency within known zones 3-5 is flat across rainfall bands (zone 4: 25.7 / 24.9 / 24.8 per 1,000). The rainfall gradient appears only for missing zone (10.9 / 17.4 / 19.3).
findings.method: Banded frequencies by zone, elevation and river distance. Separate and pooled Poisson GLMs (IRLS, log-exposure offset, year effects) with a likelihood-ratio test of equal slopes. Cross-year out-of-time deviance in emerging.
findings.implication: Flood hazard comes from the address, and the address distribution is the same as developed, so the developed flood relativities are the most transferable part of Part 1. Part 1's flood-zone 3+/missing x rainfall interaction (D-29) is, for frequency, mainly a missing-zone effect. 99% of emerging missing-zone exposure is above 1,000 mm, so a linear term would add unsupported flood load.
findings.adjustment: Carry over the zone, elevation and river relativities as frozen offsets and estimate only the flood level on emerging. Cap rainfall in the interaction at the developed 99th percentile (1,774 mm; 4.4% of 2025 test rows exceed it, 1.7% in zone 3+ or missing), or restrict the interaction to missing zone.

check.note: Core results reproduce. Banded buildings flood within zone 3+/missing: elevation <3 m 26.1 vs 29.6 per 1,000, 3-8 m 5.2 vs 5.2; river <0.5 km 25.7 vs 29.5, 0.5-2 km 11.0 vs 10.6. Developed zone rates on emerging exposure: 92.5 expected vs 80 observed (A/E 0.865) for buildings; 81.4-81.5 vs 86 (1.057) for contents. Out-of-time with developed zone relativities fixed and level matched: +127.8/+95.2 (buildings), +75.6/+166.0 (contents). Adding an emerging rain slope: -0.0/+0.3 and -3.1/-2.0. 99.1% of missing-zone exposure is above 1,000 mm. 4.4% of test rows are above 1,774 mm (1.7% in zone 3+/missing). Some figures are off; see the corrected evidence.
check.corrected_evidence: LR test of equal zone + rain slopes across markets (6 df): p=0.34 for buildings and 0.36 for contents (not 0.29/0.37). Missing-zone relativity vs zone 1: emerging buildings x40 (zone + rain GLM; raw x43), not x56, against developed x38. It rests on 8 zone-1 and 14 missing-zone claims (log se 0.45). Contents: x31-34 vs x33. Region factors on top of developed zones: -3.2/-7.2; region-only: -4.2/-8.3. Developed rain bands (<1,000 / 1,000-1,500 / 1,500+ mm): zone 4 25.7/25.2/23.3; missing zone 11.0/17.6/20.5. Same pattern as claimed. 'Rainfall adds nothing' is an out-of-time result, not a measured zero. In-sample, emerging rain slopes are +0.56 (se 0.44) per 1,000 mm for buildings and +0.78 (0.41) for contents. Both are unstable across years: 0.39 vs 0.19 for buildings and 0.99 vs -0.21 for contents, fitting on 2023 vs 2024.

findings.title: Subsidence: the clay x dry summer interaction holds in emerging and is best carried over from developed
findings.evidence: Clay at a dry summer index of 0.8 or more: 10.4 per 1,000 (15 claims) vs 8.95 in developed. Non-clay soils are flat at 1.4-1.6 per 1,000 vs 1.1-1.4. GLM coefficients, emerging vs developed: clay x (index - 0.6) 5.71 (se 2.24) vs 3.12 (0.25); clay main effect 0.23 (0.45) vs 1.00 (0.06). Joint test of equality p = 0.15, or 0.67 with region effects. The implied clay relativity at an index of 0.9 is x6.96 vs x6.95; at 0.7 it is x2.2 vs x3.7. Out-of-time: developed shape held fixed +18.3 / +5.7, emerging-fitted +14.7 / +5.8, region factors -1.0 / -23.9. Emerging 2024 subsidence is 1.65 per 1,000 against 2.81 in 2023, although the weather predicts +5%. That implies about 56% of 2024 is reported, close to Part 1's 59% for developed 2024. 2025 has lower dry summer indices (0.605 vs 0.695 exposure-weighted), so the developed shape gives subsidence frequency x0.88 against training (x0.74 on the emerging fit). By region this ranges from x0.62 (E02) to x1.69 (E05).
findings.method: Banded frequency by soil and dry summer index. Separate and pooled Poisson GLMs with LR tests. Cross-year out-of-time deviance. The 2025 multiplier is the exposure-weighted mean of exp(shape) on test rows divided by the same on training rows.
findings.implication: There are only 52 claims, so the emerging data can confirm the direction but not the size: it could only detect a slope difference above about 4.5 on the log scale. The developed interaction is the better estimate. Emerging 2024 is immature in the same way as developed.
findings.adjustment: Carry over the developed clay x dry summer interaction as a fixed offset. Develop emerging 2024 subsidence with Bornhuetter-Ferguson as in Part 1 (D-17). Price 2025 on each address's 2025 dry summer index, not region averages.

check.note: Reproduced exactly. Clay at DSI >= 0.8: 10.40 per 1,000 (15 claims) vs 8.95. Non-clay 1.39-1.59 vs 1.13-1.36. Coefficients: clay x (DSI-0.6) 5.71 (2.24) vs 3.12 (0.25); clay main effect 0.23 (0.45) vs 1.00 (0.06). Joint 4-df test p=0.151, or 0.672 with region effects. Clay relativity at 0.9 is x6.98 vs x6.95; at 0.7 x2.23 vs x3.73. Frequency 2.81 (2023) vs 1.65 (2024); the developed shape predicts +5.0%, which implies 56% reported. Exposure-weighted DSI 0.605 (test) vs 0.695 (train). 2025 multiplier x0.886 on the developed shape, x0.754 on the emerging fit; by region 0.63 (E02) to 1.66 (E05). Smaller differences: out-of-time developed-fixed +17.7/+7.0, emerging-fitted +14.7/+2.3, region-only -1.1/-32.1. The 2023-scored values differ from those stated but favour the developed shape more. Caveats: (a) a 2-df test on clay and clay x DSI alone gives p=0.049 without region effects (0.44 with), so emerging is borderline different on the clay terms. (b) Report lags: 69% of emerging 2023 subsidence claims were reported by end-2023. A one-year-old cohort would therefore be about 65-70% reported by count, above the 56% implied. The rest of the 2024 shortfall is within Poisson noise on 20 claims, but it is not established that all of it is IBNR.

findings.title: Hail drives motor glass and buildings storm; the developed curve transfers only on the right scale
findings.evidence: Glass frequency by hail band, developed vs emerging, per 1,000: 0-2 days 12.2 / 13.7; 6-9 days 21.1 / 20.1; 10-14 days 28.3 / 30.9; 15-19 days 34.8 / 40.3; 20-29 days 41.1 / 43.8. At 30+ days emerging has 66.4 (7.6% of training exposure), where developed has only 78 exposure-years. Fitting on developed and scoring emerging gives A/E 0.745 overall (0.40 at 30+) for a log-linear term in hail days, 1.084 (0.8-1.3 across bands) for log(hail+1), and 1.164 (2.03 at 30+) for XGBoost. Elasticity on log(hail+1): emerging 0.73 (se 0.055), or 0.82 with region effects, vs developed 0.53 (0.014). Out-of-time: developed log(hail+1) held fixed +50.1 / +123.5, emerging-fitted +39.6 / +124.9, developed log-linear in days -47.8 / +28.8 (fails). Buildings storm: the developed log-linear wind + hail model transfers with A/E 1.105 (2023 1.11, 2024 1.10), against 1.265 for XGBoost (1.46 at 20-29 hail days, 1.93 at 30+). With region effects the slopes are equal (p = 0.33; wind 0.151 vs 0.132, hail per 10 days 0.242 vs 0.335). Out-of-time, the developed shape held fixed gives +32.8 / +31.3, against +36.4 / +35.7 for the emerging fit. Glass/hail is 6.5% of emerging motor reported cost (26 of 407 per unit of exposure). The Part 1 motor model has no weather terms.
findings.method: Banded frequency by hail days. Poisson GLMs and a Poisson XGBoost (depth 3, early stopping on developed 2024) fitted on developed and used to predict emerging, with A/E by band. Pooled LR tests. Cross-year out-of-time deviance.
findings.implication: The hail curve carries over in level where the markets overlap. Getting its shape wrong at the high end swings emerging glass predictions by up to 5x in the 30+ band, and biases any emerging level factor calibrated on 2023-24.
findings.adjustment: Add hail to emerging motor, at least for the glass/hail peril, as log(hail+1). Credibility-blend the elasticity between developed (0.53-0.58) and emerging (0.73-0.82); 1,345 claims give the emerging value substantial weight. For storm, carry the developed log-linear wind + hail and recalibrate the level (about x1.10). Do not let trees clamp.

check.note: Confirmed parts. Glass bands, developed vs emerging: 12.2/13.7, 21.1/20.1, 28.2/30.9, 34.8/40.3, 41.1/43.8. Emerging 30+ band: 66.4 per 1,000 on 7.6% of exposure; developed has 78 exposure-years there. log(hail+1) elasticity 0.72-0.73 (se 0.054), 0.82 with region, vs developed 0.52-0.53 (0.014), 0.58 with region. Glass out-of-time: developed log(h+1) +49.8/+119.4, emerging-fitted +39.6/+124.9. Storm slopes with region effects: wind 0.151 vs 0.132, hail per 10 days 0.242 vs 0.335, p=0.33. Storm emerging-fitted out-of-time +36.4/+35.7. Glass is 6.5% of emerging motor reported cost (26.3 of 406.9 per unit of exposure). The Part 1 motor model has no weather terms (docs 4.3). Several transfer and storm figures do not hold; see the corrected evidence.
check.corrected_evidence: Glass: emerging elasticity is significantly steeper than developed. Pooled LR p=0.0004 with or without region effects (difference 0.20-0.25, se 0.06), so the developed curve does not transfer in shape even on log(hail+1). Developed-to-emerging A/E: log-linear in days 0.81 (0.47 at 30+); log(h+1) 1.13 (0.78-1.39 by band, 1.39 at 30+); hail-only XGBoost (depth 3, early stop on developed 2024) 1.06-1.10 (1.24-1.53 at 30+); seven-weather XGBoost 1.11 (1.86 at 30+). The 30+ swing is 3-4x, not 5x. A hail-only tree does no worse than log(h+1) at 30+; all developed-fitted curves under-predict the emerging high-hail tail. Developed log-linear-in-days out-of-time is -24.6/+55.6, so it fails in one direction only. Storm: without region effects the slopes differ (p=0.01; wind 0.110 vs 0.154, hail per 10 days 0.174 vs 0.319). Developed GLM transfer A/E is 1.09 with region-model slopes (1.12/1.06) and 1.19 without. Both under-predict high hail: A/E 1.21-1.39 at 20-29 days and 1.23-1.52 at 30+. Storm XGBoost gives 1.10-1.14, not 1.265; not reproduced. Developed-fixed storm out-of-time is +31.1/+30.0 to +35.3/+34.3, below the emerging fit's +36.4/+35.7 in both directions. The evidence favours estimating or blending the storm hail slope on emerging, not carrying the developed one with only a level factor.

findings.title: 2025 weather differs from 2023-24, and weather explains the emerging year-to-year changes; do not take a trend from the raw two years
findings.evidence: Test against training, exposure-weighted: hail 11.4 vs 15.6 days; hail of 20+ days on 7.7% vs 27.4%, and 30+ days on 0.6% vs 7.5%; dry summer index 0.605 vs 0.695 (0.8 or more on 10% vs 24%); freezing days 28.9 vs 19.2 (30+ on 48% vs 20%); rainfall 1,251 vs 1,380 mm; wildfire 0.528 vs 0.527; wind 5.11 vs 5.08. 2025 frequency multipliers against training, using developed shapes: glass x0.86 (x0.82 from emerging bands), storm x0.90 (x0.85), subsidence x0.88 (x0.74), escape of water x1.09 buildings and x1.12 contents, fire x1.00, flood about x1.00. Weighted by peril cost, line-level net effects are small: buildings x0.99, contents x1.02, motor x0.99. 2024 against 2023 in emerging, predicted from weather vs observed: storm +15.2% vs +13.7%; glass +13.2% vs +16.2%; buildings escape of water -3.2% vs -1.6%; contents escape of water -4.5% vs -6.7%. Illustration: projecting 2024 forward by the 2023-to-2024 change gives 2025 glass 43.0 per 1,000 against 29.7 weather-based (x1.45), and storm 23.9 against 17.8 (x1.34).
findings.method: Exposure-weighted weather summaries on test vs training rows. The multiplier is the mean of exp(peril shape) on test rows divided by the same on training rows. Peril reported cost per unit of exposure is used as the weight. Predicted year ratios use the same shapes on each year's rows.
findings.implication: With two years, the year-on-year change in emerging frequency is weather, not trend. A trend fitted on emerging 2023-24 without weather terms would overshoot hail and storm perils in a mild-hail 2025. At row and region level the 2025 weather effect is large even though the line totals barely move.
findings.adjustment: Price each 2025 row on its address's 2025 weather. Take the claims-inflation trend from Part 1 (it is net of weather) or from the cost lens, never from raw emerging 2023-24. Calibrate the emerging level only after the weather adjustment.

check.note: Test vs training weather reproduces exactly (exposure-weighted, buildings). Hail 11.4 vs 15.6 days; 20+ days 7.7% vs 27.4%; 30+ 0.6% vs 7.5%; DSI 0.605 vs 0.695 (>=0.8 on 10% vs 24%); freezing 28.9 vs 19.2 (30+ on 48% vs 20%); rain 1,251 vs 1,380; wildfire 0.528 vs 0.527; wind 5.11 vs 5.08. Multipliers depend somewhat on specification: glass x0.87 (developed) / x0.82 (emerging bands); storm x0.89-0.92 / x0.85; subsidence x0.89 / x0.75; escape of water x1.10 (buildings) and x1.14 (contents); fire x1.00. 2024 vs 2023, predicted vs observed: storm +14% to +20% vs +13.7%; glass +12.6% vs +16.2%; buildings EoW -3.6% vs -1.7%; contents EoW -4.9% vs -6.7%. Illustration: glass 43.0 vs about 30 per 1,000; storm 23.9 vs about 18. Two claims are overstated; see the corrected evidence.
check.corrected_evidence: Weather explains the 2023-to-2024 change only for storm, glass and escape of water. Changes not explained by weather: fire -60% (weather predicts +5%); subsidence -41% (+5%); flood -15% (buildings) and -35% (contents); motor own damage -11.8%; third-party property -9.9%; bodily injury -35%. These reflect IBNR, volatility or a non-weather change, so the reason not to trend on raw 2023-24 is broader than weather. The Part 1 trend is net of weather only for buildings. The docs say 'The trend is net of the rating factors and, for buildings, of weather.' The Part 1 contents and motor models have no weather terms, so their trends are not net of weather.

findings.title: Do not fit E01-E06 region factors: region effects in emerging are mostly weather shocks and fail out of time
findings.evidence: Region x year explains 62-89% of emerging variance in rainfall, dry summer index, freezing days, temperature and wildfire, against 54% for hail and 68% for wind. For the dry summer index, region alone explains only 22% but region x year 85%. Glass frequency moves with regional hail: E03 20.9 to 44.2 per 1,000 as hail went from 9.6 to 24.1 days; E05 55.2 to 34.4 as hail went from 28.6 to 16.7. Out-of-time, region factors worsen deviance in both directions on every peril tested: glass -142.1 / -38.8, storm -19.2 / -8.2, buildings escape of water -21.1 / -8.7, subsidence -1.0 / -23.9, fire -6.3 / -11.7, buildings flood -4.2 / -8.2, contents flood -1.8 / -3.8 (contents escape of water +1.2 / -6.6). Adding region to the climate terms also worsens storm (+27.0 / +32.4 against +36.4 / +35.7 without region). The 2025 weather shift by region ranges from x0.65 (E05) to x1.03 (E06) for glass, x0.77-1.13 for storm, x0.62-1.69 for subsidence and x0.91-1.15 for escape of water. No E region is a climatic analogue of any R region: E region-year hail means run 4-29 days against an R maximum of 10.4, and E02/E04 wildfire 0.67-0.87 against an R maximum of 0.34. E04 is 4.3% of exposure (46 buildings claims).
findings.method: Variance decomposition of address-year weather into region, region x year and within. Region x year frequency tables. Cross-year out-of-time Poisson deviance (fit one year, score the other, level matched) for region-only, climate-only and region + climate models.
findings.implication: A region factor fitted on 2023-24 absorbs that period's regional weather and misprices 2025 by the shifts above. It cannot borrow from the developed R regions either. This matches the Part 1 finding that region adds little beyond address and weather.
findings.adjustment: No region factor, or one shrunk heavily towards 1. Carry location through address features plus each year's weather. Do not map R regions to E regions.

check.note: Confirmed. Glass by region-year: E03 20.9 to 44.2 per 1,000 as hail went 9.6 to 24.2; E05 55.2 to 34.4 as hail went 28.6 to 16.8. Region-only out-of-time (level matched): glass -142.0/-38.8, storm -19.2/-8.2, buildings EoW -21.1/-8.7, fire -6.3/-11.7, buildings flood -4.2/-8.3, contents flood -1.8/-3.8, contents EoW +1.2/-6.6. Storm with climate + region: +27.0/+32.5 vs +36.4/+35.7 without region. 2025 shift by region: glass 0.66 (E05) to 1.03 (E06); subsidence 0.63-1.66; EoW 0.87-1.22; storm 0.77-1.21, depending on the slopes used. E04: 4.4% of buildings exposure, 46 claims. The conclusion stands; the figures in the corrected evidence need fixing.
check.corrected_evidence: Subsidence region-only, scored on 2023, is -32.1, not -23.9. The R comparators are multi-year region means (R07 hail 10.4, R02 wildfire 0.34), not region-year values. Like-for-like R region-year maxima are hail 11.5 days and wildfire 0.41 (2021-24), or 0.45 including 2025. The variance decomposition reproduces only with 2025 included. Region alone / region x year: rain 0.50/0.62, DSI 0.22/0.84, freezing 0.56/0.78, temperature 0.59/0.88, wildfire 0.74/0.86, hail 0.15/0.54, wind 0.58/0.68. In 2023-24 alone, region explains most of it: rain 0.49/0.53, DSI 0.61/0.83, freezing 0.61/0.72, temperature 0.81/0.87, wildfire 0.73/0.86, wind 0.60/0.69, hail 0.26/0.55. So 'mostly weather shocks' holds clearly for hail and the 2025 DSI shift, less for the rest. Region-only factors also fail out-of-time on non-weather perils: motor own damage -3.5/-2.3, third-party property -2.8/-0.5, contents theft -1.8/-4.0. Thin data, not only weather shocks, drives the failure.

findings.title: Fire and wildfire: the developed slope transfers, but emerging fire is volatile, beyond developed support and nearly half of buildings cost
findings.evidence: In developed, fire frequency rises from 1.49 to 3.06 per 1,000 between wildfire index under 0.1 and 0.4-0.5. Slope per 0.1: developed x1.19 (log-scale se 0.024), emerging x1.18 (0.072), p = 0.89; with region effects x1.155 vs x1.12 (se 0.17), p = 0.87. Within E02, index 0.67 or more gives 6.22 per 1,000 (18 claims) against 1.54 (2) below. Emerging fire frequency is 4.31 per 1,000 in 2023 and 1.74 in 2024, while the weather predicts +5%. 17 of the 2023 high-wildfire claims are in E02, spread from February to December, so this is not one event. There are 70 fire claims, of which 20 above 50k carry 75% of fire cost. Fire is 45% of emerging buildings reported cost (185 of 407 per unit of exposure): 283 in 2023 and 93 in 2024, against a stable 91-105 in developed. The developed shape transfers with A/E 0.75 (1.11 in 2023, 0.43 in 2024). Out-of-time: developed shape held fixed -2.1 / +7.0 (marginal fail), emerging-fitted -2.6 / -20.4. 20.6% of 2025 buildings test exposure is above the developed maximum of 0.669 (94% of E02, 89% of E04). Extrapolating log-linearly instead of clamping raises fire frequency 4.9% overall, 17.5% in E02 and 14.1% in E04.
findings.method: Banded fire frequency by wildfire index, within-region and by month. Separate and pooled Poisson GLMs with LR tests. Developed-to-emerging transfer A/E. Cross-year out-of-time deviance. Extrapolated vs clamped comparison as the mean of exp(1.81 x index) with and without capping at 0.669.
findings.implication: This is the main new-climate risk. The wildfire gradient is real and transferable, but the emerging fire level rests on 70 claims dominated by large losses, and one region-year (E02, 2023) drives it. The buildings level is the most uncertain part of the 2025 emerging prediction.
findings.adjustment: Carry the developed log-linear wildfire slope and extrapolate it, with a clamped variant as a sensitivity. Set the fire level from pooled 2023-24 emerging, blended by credibility with the developed-implied level, and route large fires through the Part 1 large-claim/Pareto tail. Report a wide fire-driven range for the buildings level.

check.note: Confirmed. Developed fire rises from 1.49 to 3.06 per 1,000. Slope per 0.1 of wildfire index: x1.189 (0.024) vs x1.176 (0.072), p=0.89; with region effects x1.155 vs x1.121 (0.172), p=0.87. Frequency 4.31 (2023) vs 1.74 (2024); weather predicts +4.6%. 70 claims; 20 above 50k carry 75.3% of fire cost. Fire is 185.3 of 407.3 per unit of exposure (45%): 283 in 2023, 93 in 2024, against 91-105 in developed. Transfer A/E 0.78 (1.15 / 0.44) on the developed 2023-24 level. Out-of-time: developed-fixed -2.0/+7.0, emerging-fitted -2.6/-20.3. 20.6% of test exposure is above 0.669 (94% of E02, 89% of E04). Extrapolating at a slope of 1.81 raises fire frequency 4.9% overall, 17.5% in E02 and 14.1% in E04. Some evidence is wrong; see the corrected evidence.
check.corrected_evidence: The within-E02 contrast (6.22 vs 1.54 per 1,000) is a year effect, not a wildfire gradient. Within each year the rates are similar: 2023 9.0 (>=0.67) vs 6.2 (<0.67); 2024 0.99 vs 0.88. E02's exposure below 0.67 is mostly in 2024. The 2023 spike is not one region-year: outside E02, 2023 is still 3.32 vs 1.91 per 1,000 (x1.74). The emerging-fitted slope flips sign between years: +2.06 per unit fitting on 2023, -2.08 fitting on 2024. The gradient therefore rests on developed data alone. One E02 2023 claim falls in January, so the spread is January to December. The 0.669 clamp includes the developed 2025 test-year weather. Clamping at the training maximum of 0.635 instead puts 22.1% of test exposure beyond it, and extrapolation raises fire frequency 6.7% overall, 24.7% in E02 and 20.9% in E04. A slope of 1.81 is x1.20 per 0.1, slightly above the fitted 1.73 (x1.19).

findings.title: Escape of water: the freezing-days and building-age shapes carry over, but the emerging level is about 20% lower for reasons other than climate
findings.evidence: Freezing-day slope per day: developed 0.0096, emerging 0.0109 (se 0.0051), p = 0.80. With the developed freezing shape, emerging A/E is flat across freezing bands (0.7-0.8): buildings 0.80 (0.796 in 2023, 0.809 in 2024) and contents 0.82 (0.83 / 0.81). Fewer freezing days explain part of the raw gap: raw ratio 0.68 against a climate-predicted 0.79 (buildings). Building-age gradient: pre-1919 vs 2000+ is 25.0 vs 12.2 per 1,000 in developed (2.0x) and 16.5 vs 9.1 in emerging (1.8x). For storm the gradient is 2.6x vs 2.8x. Out-of-time, the developed freezing shape held fixed gives -2.8 / +7.1 (buildings) and +3.1 / +2.7 (contents). Seasonality is the same, so this is the same hemisphere: 37% of emerging buildings escape-of-water claims fall in December to February (developed 35%), and 37% of storm claims (36%). 2025 has 50% more freezing days, so escape-of-water frequency is x1.09 (buildings) and x1.12 (contents). Escape of water is 14% of contents reported cost.
findings.method: Poisson GLMs on freezing days, developed-to-emerging transfer A/E by band, building-age banded frequency, claim counts by meteorological season, and cross-year out-of-time deviance.
findings.implication: Climate explains the shape of escape of water but not its level. The remaining x0.80 is a market difference (building stock, plumbing or claim behaviour) that only emerging data can set. Part 1's seasonal exposure weights for contents (D-22) are not contradicted.
findings.adjustment: Carry over the freezing and year-built shapes. Calibrate the emerging escape-of-water level (about x0.80 against developed at equal climate). Apply 2025 freezing days. Keep the contents seasonal weights.

check.note: Confirmed. Freezing-day slope 0.0096 vs 0.0109 (0.0051), p=0.80; contents 0.0127 vs 0.0161, p=0.59. Out-of-time with the developed freezing shape fixed: -3.1/+7.5 (buildings), +3.3/+2.8 (contents). December-February share: EoW 36.6% vs 35.5%, storm 37.3% vs 36.4%. Emerging building-age gradient 16.5 vs 9.1 per 1,000 (1.81x, excluding 1900). EoW is 14.0% of contents cost. The conclusion holds: escape-of-water level about x0.82 at equal climate. Several figures are off; see the corrected evidence.
check.corrected_evidence: A/E with the developed freezing shape and developed level: buildings 0.82 (0.81 in 2023, 0.82 in 2024); contents 0.83-0.84 (0.84-0.85 / 0.83-0.84). Raw buildings ratio 0.68 vs a climate-predicted 0.83, not 0.79. The stated 0.68/0.79 implies 0.86, which contradicts the stated A/E of 0.80. Buildings band A/E is 0.75-0.86. Contents is not flat across bands: 0.59-1.07. Developed age gradient, excluding 1900: 25.2 vs 12.8 per 1,000 (1.97x); raw 23.9 vs 12.8. Storm age gradient: developed 2.4x, emerging 2.8x. 2025 multipliers: x1.10 (buildings) and x1.14 (contents) on developed slopes; x1.12 / x1.18 on emerging slopes.

findings.title: Data volume limits what emerging can estimate: freeze developed shapes and estimate only levels and a few well-supported terms
findings.evidence: Emerging buildings has 23,468 exposure-years and 1,056 claims, against about 600,000 and 26,266 in developed (about 4%). By peril: flood 80, subsidence 52, fire 70, storm 464, glass/hail 1,345. Emerging standard errors are about 0.55 on log-scale zone relativities (a factor of 1.7 at one standard error), 2.24 against 0.25 on clay x dry summer, and 0.055 against 0.014 on hail elasticity. Regional weather shocks come from only 12 region-year cells. A free fit of all seven weather variables on emerging gives spurious effects on a non-weather peril: accidental damage shows wildfire z = 3.1 and dry summer z = 2.6, with temperature coefficients of -2.2 and -3.9 on accidental damage and flood that have no developed counterpart. Developed-fixed shapes match or beat emerging-fitted ones out of time on flood, subsidence, storm and glass.
findings.method: Claim and exposure counts by peril. GLM standard errors from separate fits. A seven-variable Poisson GLM per peril in each market, as an overfitting check.
findings.implication: "Consistent with developed" here means "not contradicted", not "confirmed equal". Weather and regional effects fitted freely on emerging capture region and customer confounding.
findings.adjustment: Use developed climate and address relativities as fixed offsets. Estimate on emerging only peril-level calibration factors (with credibility) and, where claims support it, the glass hail elasticity. Report the 2025 range with separate contributions from the fire level, hail and wildfire extrapolation choices and the subsidence BF prior.

check.note: Confirmed. Emerging buildings: 23,468 exposure-years and 1,056 claims, vs 590,560 and 26,266 in developed (4.0%). Peril counts: flood 80, subsidence 52, fire 70, storm 464, glass 1,345. Standard errors: zone relativities 0.42-0.61; 2.24 vs 0.25 on clay x DSI; 0.054 vs 0.014 on hail elasticity. 12 region-year cells. Seven-variable GLM: buildings accidental damage gets wildfire z=3.1, DSI z=2.6 and temperature -2.19 (z=-2.3); flood gets temperature -3.86 (z=-3.3). Developed equivalents are +0.10 and -0.00. One headline claim is wrong; see the corrected evidence.
check.corrected_evidence: 'Developed-fixed shapes match or beat emerging-fitted ones out of time on flood, subsidence, storm and glass' is false for storm and mixed for glass. Storm, emerging-fitted: +36.4/+35.7, beating developed-fixed (+31.1/+30.0 to +35.3/+34.3) in both directions. Glass: developed-fixed +49.8/+119.4 vs emerging-fitted +39.6/+124.9. The claim holds for flood: developed zones +127.8/+95.2 vs emerging-fitted zones +117.9/-65.4 (buildings). It holds for subsidence: +17.7/+7.0 vs +14.7/+2.3. Storm hail and wind slopes also differ significantly without region effects (p=0.01), and glass elasticity differs at p=0.0004. The terms estimated on emerging should therefore include the storm hail slope as well as the glass elasticity.

findings.title: Expense table: emerging loads are heavier and must stay out of the scored prediction; there is no commission rate for comparison-site business
findings.evidence: Fact (expenses table, developed / emerging): fixed expense per policy 45 / 85 CU; variable expense 12% / 15%; broker commission 15% / 20%; comparison-site commission 10% / NaN; direct commission 0 / 0; premium tax 12% / 8%; cat reinsurance 6% / 12% of property risk premium; target profit 5% / 8%. Under the build-up P = (RP x (1 + cat load for buildings and contents) + fixed) / (1 - variable - commission - tax - profit), the denominator is 0.56 / 0.49 for broker business and 0.71 / 0.69 for direct business. An emerging broker policy therefore costs 2.04 x RP + 173 CU (motor) or 2.29 x RP + 173 CU (home), against 1.79 x RP + 80 CU in the developed market. Illustration using observed, undeveloped 2023-24 cost per unit of exposure as RP: an emerging broker contents policy (RP 89) costs about 377 CU, of which claims are 24%; the developed equivalent (RP 117) costs 302 CU, of which claims are 39%. Emerging broker motor (RP 407): 1,004 CU, claims 40%. Comparison-site business is 5.0% of the emerging test rows (4,530 motor, 2,624 buildings and 3,304 contents; 10,458 in total) and 4.9% of motor training rows, yet the table gives no commission for it. Fixed expense is per policy, but motor has 90,521 test rows on 83,907 policies, and 11.6% of motor, 8.1% of buildings and 9.7% of contents test rows are under half a year.
findings.method: Read e_expenses directly. Channel counts are from the policy and test files. The build-up formula is my assumption, because the table states units but not how the items combine. RP is the sum of net incurred (excluding repudiated claims) divided by exposure recomputed as (end - start + 1) / 365.
findings.implication: The scored target is the risk premium (the competition says it is not the premium charged), so none of these loads should touch the submission. They matter for the pricing tool and the reference policies. The doubled cat load is the insurer's own signal that property results are more volatile, which should widen the stated uncertainty for buildings and contents. It is not a reason to change the expected cost.
findings.adjustment: None to the 2025 predictions. In the pricing tool: apply the emerging column; apply fixed expense once per policy, not per row, so part-year rows do not take a full 85 CU each; set an explicit, documented comparison-site commission assumption (for example the developed 10% or the broker 20%) and flag it as a gap in the data.

check.note: Everything re-derived matches. e_expenses: fixed 45/85, variable 12%/15%, broker 15%/20%, comparison 10%/NaN, direct 0/0, tax 12%/8%, cat 6%/12% of property RP, profit 5%/8%. Denominators: broker 0.56/0.49, direct 0.71/0.69. Raw RP (net incurred minus recoveries, repudiated and duplicate claims excluded, claims joined on policy_id with loss_date inside the row, exposure recomputed): emerging contents 88.9, developed contents 116.9, emerging motor 406.9. Built-up premiums are 377 CU (claims 24%), 302 CU (39%) and 1,004 CU (41%). Comparison-site rows: 4,530 motor, 2,624 buildings, 3,304 contents, 10,458 of 209,063 test rows (5.0%); 4.9% of motor training rows. Motor test file: 90,521 rows on 83,907 policies. Rows under half a year: 11.6% motor, 8.1% buildings, 9.7% contents. The brief does say the target 'is the risk premium, not the premium charged'. One wording point: '1.79 x RP + 80' is the developed motor formula. Developed home is 1.89 x RP + 80, which is what the 302 CU illustration actually uses. Context worth adding: comparison site is 35.0% of developed motor rows (342,826 of 979,968) against 5% in emerging, so the gap in the table matters less here than it would in Part 1.

findings.title: The 20 reference policies are exact copies of test rows, chosen to exercise the premium build-up
findings.evidence: Fact: 7 motor, 7 buildings and 6 contents rows. Every row_id is in the matching test file, and every field matches the test row exactly (34 motor fields, 25 buildings, 26 contents), so they carry no extra information such as a target. All fall in 2025. Channels: 17 broker, 3 direct, 0 comparison site. 18 of the 20 are new business, and only 2 of the 20 customers (1 motor, 1 contents) appear anywhere in the 2023-24 training data. Two rows are part-year (exposures 0.07 and 0.11). Three of the 7 motor rows are in the 17-24 band. Gender: motor 5 men and 2 women, buildings 3 and 4, contents 0 men and 6 women. Buildings rows use the emerging construction codes (BRK, WOD, MIX, STN), not the Part 1 codes (brick, stone, timber, non-standard). None has a sum insured error of 1,000 times or a missed payment.
findings.method: Joined the reference policies to the test files on row_id and compared every column cell by cell (nulls treated as equal). Profiled channel, new business, exposure, age band and gender in aggregate, and checked which customer and policy IDs appear in the training data.
findings.implication: Inference: these are worked examples for the pricing-tool deliverable. They would show the risk premium, then the expense, commission, tax, cat and profit loads, for a mix the broker book dominates. Several features make the reference set sensitive to modelling choices: mostly new business with no claims history, young drivers, part-year rows, and an all-female contents subset. The gender decision changes every contents reference premium by about 11-13%.
findings.adjustment: Produce a premium build-up table for the 20 rows from the final model, with and without gender, and show the part-year and fixed-expense handling. Map the construction codes to Part 1 levels before reusing any Part 1 relativity.

check.note: Confirmed: 7/7/6 rows; every row_id is in its test file with zero cell mismatches (34/25/26 fields); all rows in 2025; 17 broker, 3 direct, 0 comparison site; 18 of 20 new business; 2 of 20 customers (1 motor, 1 contents) in training; 3 of 7 motor rows aged 17-24; gender M/F 5/2, 3/4, 0/6; no x1000 sum insured (max 378k buildings, 71k contents); no missed payments. Three points are off, listed below.
check.corrected_evidence: Part-year: three rows are under half a year, not two: exposures 0.07 (contents), 0.11 (buildings) and 0.33 (motor). 15 of the 20 rows are below a full year. Construction: the reference buildings rows use only BRK (4), MIX (2) and WOD (1). STN occurs in the emerging data (2,170 training and 4,117 test rows) but not in the reference set. Gender effect: the 11-13% applies to the risk premium. My GLMs, fitted with and without gender, move the six all-female contents rows' risk premium by -11% to -13% (written-premium spec) or -11% to -21% (full spec). After the build-up ((RP x 1.12 + 85) / 0.49 for broker), the 85 CU fixed expense dilutes this to about -4% to -10% on the charged premium, and under 1% on the 0.07-exposure row.

findings.title: Gender is strongly predictive in motor, moderately in contents (women cost more) and not in buildings
findings.evidence: Motor, raw (2023-24): men 204.5 claims per 1,000 against women 157.7 (x1.30); cost per unit of exposure 467 against 348 (x1.34). The effect holds in both years (cost x1.27 in 2023, x1.42 in 2024) and in all six regions (cost x1.15 to x1.57). It comes from accident perils: men have more bodily injury, third-party property and own-damage claims (278/171, 1,281/912 and 1,499/1,173 claims), while glass and theft are similar. Multivariate GLM with 24 rating factors: frequency x1.33 (95% CI 1.26-1.39), cost x1.36 (1.19-1.54). Out-of-time Tweedie D2 gain from adding gender is positive in every specification and both directions: +0.0043 (2023 to 2024, customer-bootstrap 95% CI +0.0017 to +0.0074) and +0.0043 (2024 to 2023, CI -0.0022 to +0.0122) on the ridge GLM, and +0.0034 and +0.0023 on a written-premium-only model. Contents: women cost x1.33 more (GLM men/women 0.75, CI 0.61-0.93), mainly through severity: escape of water median 1,641 against 1,258, theft 2,305 against 1,743. The frequency effect is not significant (0.93, CI 0.83-1.06). D2 gain +0.0023 to +0.0035 in all four tests, though every bootstrap interval includes zero. Buildings: frequency x1.10 (CI 0.97-1.25), cost x0.96 (CI 0.69-1.34), and out-of-time D2 is worse with gender (-0.0018 to -0.0035).
findings.method: Own IRLS log-link GLMs (Poisson for frequency, Tweedie p=1.5 for cost) with a log-exposure offset, on emerging 2023-24 rows. The target is raw net incurred: no development, and repudiated claims are excluded. Banded rating factors, and sum insured divided by 1,000 above 1m (contents) or 10m (buildings). Out-of-time: fit one year, score the other, rebalanced to the actual total so that only ranking is compared. 500-draw customer-cluster bootstrap of the deviance difference.
findings.implication: In motor the gain is large by Part 1 standards: claim history added about 0.004 to motor D2 in Part 1, and the trend 0.0009. Gender is the strongest single new signal in the emerging data. No relativity can come from Part 1, because the developed data has no gender field.
findings.adjustment: If gender is used, use it in motor (and contents, with shrinkage given the wide interval) and leave it out of buildings. Estimate it on emerging data only, with the age interaction set out in the separate finding on age and gender.

check.note: Motor and contents reproduce closely. Motor raw figures: 204.5 against 157.7 claims per 1,000 (x1.30); cost per unit of exposure 467 against 348 (x1.34); x1.27 in 2023 and x1.42 in 2024; regions x1.15 to x1.57. Peril claim counts are exactly 278/171, 1,281/912 and 1,499/1,173. My 24-factor IRLS GLMs give frequency x1.32 (CI 1.26-1.39) and cost x1.35 (1.19-1.54). Out-of-time gain from gender, ridge GLM: +0.0049 (CI +0.0009 to +0.0085) and +0.0026 (-0.0052 to +0.0095); written-premium model +0.0036 and +0.0023. Contents: raw women/men 101.8 against 75.9 (x1.34); GLM cost 0.74 (CI 0.61-0.90), frequency 0.94 (0.83-1.06); gains +0.0024 to +0.0049, every interval includes zero. Two parts are overstated, listed below.

The point estimate depends on the specification and both intervals include 1. Out-of-time D2 from gender is mixed, not consistently worse: 2023 to 2024 gives +0.0016 (ridge 100), +0.0011 (ridge 1,000) and 0.0000 (written premium); 2024 to 2023 gives -0.0077, -0.0047 and -0.0036.
