findings.title: Using or excluding gender is a governance decision; the current tariff is gender-neutral, and occupation partly proxies for gender
findings.evidence: Fact: since 21 December 2012 (the Test-Achats ruling, which applies Directive 2004/113/EC and is retained in UK law), UK and EU insurers may not differentiate individual premiums by gender. The Commission's 2012 guidelines still allow gender in aggregate risk assessment and reserving. The emerging market's rule is not stated. Data: the insurer's current emerging written premium is almost gender-neutral after controlling for rating factors (a male effect on log written premium of +0.6% on training rows and +0.5% on test rows for motor, +0.1% for contents, about -1% to -3% for buildings), against a true motor cost relativity of x1.33. Excluding gender barely moves the test totals (under 0.35% on every line), because test rows are 50.0% male in motor (49.4% in training), 50.1% in buildings and 50.0% in contents. It does move individuals. Motor: men -11% to -12% at the median, women +13% to +16%. Contents: men +13% to +18%, women -11% to -13%. Buildings: plus or minus 2% to 6%, with an unstable sign. Proxy: once gender is dropped, the base factors carry no gender signal (fitted men/women 0.99 motor, 1.00 contents). Adding occupation, which is heavily gendered (mechanic 95% male, hairdresser 5%), pulls back about 20% of the motor log-effect (fitted men/women 1.06 against 1.33) and about 8% for contents.
findings.method: OLS of log written premium on the same rating factors plus a male flag, on training and test rows. GLM predictions with and without gender for every test row, fitted on 2023-24 with three specifications (written premium only, base factors, base plus cleaned occupation); reports the median of the row ratio by gender. Occupation was cleaned by lower-casing, trimming and splitting off the 'Self-employed ' prefix, which takes 81 raw values to 20 levels.
findings.implication: Inference: the dataset supplies gender while withholding credit band and date of birth. That is consistent with a regime that permits gender rating, but nothing in the brief or data confirms it. The strongest case against using gender: it is unlawful in the team's home jurisdictions and contrary to UK and EU norms, and the contents effect is not robust. The strongest case for: the score measures predictive accuracy only, and the motor effect is large, significant and stable. If gender is excluded, occupation becomes an indirect proxy that a fairness review would flag.
findings.adjustment: Make it an explicit, documented decision with both versions run. Recommended: model expected cost with gender for motor (and contents, shrunk) for the scored submission, as aggregate risk assessment, and quote any customer-facing premium in the pricing tool on a gender-neutral basis unless the emerging rule is confirmed. Report the cost of neutrality: about -0.003 to -0.004 D2 in motor and about -0.003 in contents. If gender is excluded, test and cap occupation's proxy effect.

check.note: The conclusions hold. Differences are at specification level only. OLS of log written premium on the rating factors plus a male flag: motor +0.27% (training) and +0.22% (test), against the stated +0.6% and +0.5%; contents +0.10% and +0.15%; buildings -0.6% and -0.2%, against the stated -1% to -3%. Either way the tariff is essentially gender-neutral. Male shares: motor test 50.0%, training 49.4%; buildings test 50.1%; contents test 50.0%. Excluding gender changes the test totals by +0.09% to -0.38% across lines and specifications. Median row ratio without/with gender: motor men 0.875-0.893, women 1.132-1.169; contents men 1.174-1.184, women 0.867-0.873; buildings 0.95-1.07. With gender dropped, fitted men/women is 1.00 (motor) and 0.98 (contents). Adding cleaned occupation gives 1.07 in motor (about 21% of log 1.33, as stated) and 0.96 in contents (about 14% of the log effect against the stated 8%). Occupation cleaning: 80 non-null raw values (81 with null) become 40 after lower-casing and trimming, and 20 after splitting off 'self-employed'. Mechanic is 94.5% male on motor training rows; hairdresser is 6.3% male there and 9.9% across all customers, not 5%. The legal points are correct: Test-Achats (C-236/09) effective 21 December 2012 under Directive 2004/113/EC, and the Commission's 2012 guidelines allow aggregate use.

findings.title: The gender effect is concentrated in young drivers, and the 2025 broker book over-weights them
findings.evidence: Raw men/women frequency by driver age band: 1.70 (17-24), 1.40 (25-34), 1.08 (35-49), 0.97 (50-64), 1.14 (65+). Multivariate, with all other factors: frequency 1.78, 1.40, 1.11, 1.00, 1.14; cost 1.81, 1.41, 1.15, 1.06, 1.23. Out of time, a gender-by-age term beats a single gender term in both directions on the written-premium model: cost D2 +0.0005 (2023 to 2024) and +0.0045 (2024 to 2023), frequency +0.0041 and +0.0039. On the heavily shrunk full GLM the cost result is mixed (-0.0017 and +0.0020). The 17-24 band is 24.8% of 2025 motor test rows against 19.9% of training rows, and 84.5% of the 2025 17-24 rows are new business. The male share is about 50% in every test band.
findings.method: Raw ratios by band and gender. A Poisson or Tweedie GLM with a combined gender-and-age-band factor (women 35-49 as the base) and all other motor factors. Fit one year and score the other, rebalanced. Band shares from the test file.
findings.implication: A single gender relativity (x1.33) under-prices young men by roughly 35% and over-prices men aged 50-64 by about 25%. Where it matters most is the young segment the new broker book is heavy in. Equally, excluding gender takes out the largest price differences in that segment, which is where any adverse selection against a neutral tariff would appear.
findings.adjustment: If gender is used: model gender by age band (at least 17-24, 25-34 and 35+), with credibility shrinkage towards the main effect. If not: say plainly that the young-male cross-subsidy is concentrated in about a quarter of the 2025 motor book.

check.note: The descriptive figures replicate. Raw men/women frequency by band: 1.70, 1.40, 1.08, 0.97, 1.14. Joint GLM (women 35-49 as base): frequency 1.76, 1.40, 1.11, 0.99, 1.14; cost 1.80, 1.42, 1.15, 1.07, 1.22. The 17-24 band is 24.8% of test rows against 19.9% of training rows; 84.5% of 2025 rows aged 17-24 are new business; the male share is 49.6-50.7% in every band. The out-of-time cost result and the size of the mis-pricing do not hold, as set out below.
check.corrected_evidence: Out of time, I did not reproduce the cost gain. Moving from 'written premium + age + gender' to 'written premium + gender x age band' changes Tweedie D2 by -0.0034 (2023 to 2024) and -0.0007 (2024 to 2023). Against 'written premium + gender' with no age term it is -0.0030 and -0.0068. On the full ridge GLM it is -0.0041 and -0.0010 (ridge 100), and -0.0038 and -0.0008 (ridge 1,000). Only frequency improves: +0.0020 and +0.0023 (written-premium model), +0.0017 and +0.0019 (ridge 100), and -0.0007 and -0.0011 (ridge 1,000). The interaction is supported in frequency, not in cost. Mis-pricing is overstated by two to three times. I fitted single-gender and gender-by-age Tweedie GLMs on 2023-24 data. The single relativity prices young men about 12% below the interaction model (actual/expected 1.09) and men aged 50-64 about 12% above it (actual/expected 0.88). It over-prices women aged 17-24 by about 17% (actual/expected 0.84). The ratio gap between 1.81 and 1.33 is split between men and women, through the age main effect; it is not borne by men alone.

findings.title: Missing credit band: modest predictive loss, partly recovered through missed payments and payment method
findings.evidence: Developed (Part 1) data: credit band E (8.1% of motor rows) has a frequency of 180 per 1,000 against 135-143 for A-D (x1.31). Contents E is x1.37 (53.3 against 38-40) and buildings E x1.29 (56.1 against 42-45); bands A-D are flat. Adding credit band to an emerging-style GLM on developed data (fit 2021-22, score 2023) adds Tweedie D2 +0.0006 (motor) and +0.0004 (contents), and -0.0003 for buildings. Proxies that remain in emerging: in developed data, 41% of band-E customers have a missed payment (2% for band A) and 75% pay monthly (40% for A). The emerging missed-payment relativity is somewhat steeper: motor frequency 251 against 175 per 1,000 for one missed payment (x1.43), against x1.32 in developed. The share with any missed payment is the same in both markets (7.9% emerging, 8.2% developed). Part 1 used credit band in both the motor and contents GLMs.
findings.method: Univariate rates by credit band (developed 2021-24). Tweedie GLMs on developed data with and without credit band, using only the factors available in emerging. Cross-tabulation of credit band against missed payments and monthly payment. Matching emerging univariate rates.
findings.implication: Inference: the absence is consistent either with regulation (some jurisdictions restrict credit-based insurance scores) or with a thin credit bureau, which is common in emerging markets. Either way the Part 1 credit relativities cannot be carried over. The lost signal is small, and missed payments and payment method partly absorb it, so their emerging relativities should not be forced back to Part 1 values.
findings.adjustment: Drop credit band. Let missed payments and payment method be fitted freely on emerging data, or with a Part 1 prior allowed to steepen. Document that this is a likely proxy, so a fairness review knows about it.

check.note: The numbers hold. Developed motor credit band E is 8.1% of rows, with frequency 180 against 135-143 for A-D. Contents E is 53.3 against 38-40; buildings E is 56.1 against 42-45. Band E: 41% have a missed payment (A: 2%) and 75% pay monthly (A: 40%). Missed payments, 1 against 0: emerging 251 against 175 per 1,000 (x1.43), developed x1.32. Any missed payment in 2023-24: 7.9% emerging, 8.2% developed. Adding credit band to an emerging-style GLM (fit 2021-22, score 2023) gains +0.0007 in motor, +0.0005 in contents and -0.0005 in buildings, close to the stated figures. Part 1 used credit band in both the motor and contents GLMs (documentation sections 4.1 and 4.3). The proxy list, however, leaves out the most direct proxy.
check.corrected_evidence: Marketing segment is a direct credit proxy and is present in the emerging customer file. In the developed customers (545,240), the segment tier maps exactly onto credit band: affluent = A/B, mainstream = C, budget = D/E. Part 1 documentation section 5.9 records this aliasing. The emerging budget tier is 20.0% of customers, against 20.1% developed. On 2023-24 data its motor frequency is 210 against 173-174 per 1,000 (x1.21), and contents 45.3 against 29.2-36.9. In developed motor, adding the tier recovers +0.0002 of the +0.0005 credit gain, measured excluding the single 11.9m claim. The rest is the D-against-E split. The adjustment should treat marketing segment as an explicit credit proxy, alongside missed payments and payment method, both for modelling and for fairness review. If credit rating is restricted in this market, using segment would circumvent the restriction.

findings.title: Age bands in place of exact age: little information lost; the Part 1 age shape carries over, and years licensed restores much of the detail within each band
findings.evidence: Fact: the emerging data has driver_age_band and policyholder_age_band (17-24, 25-34, 35-49, 50-64, 65+) and no date_of_birth. On developed data, moving from fine age bands to these five bands costs Tweedie D2 0.0012 in motor (0.0856 to 0.0844; frequency 0.1145 to 0.1121) and 0.0002 in contents; buildings improves by 0.0023, because fine bands overfit. Motor frequency relativity by band, developed / emerging: 1.72 / 1.53, 1.10 / 1.06, 0.81 / 0.78, 0.72 / 0.72, 0.91 / 0.89. Contents is similar at 17-24 (1.31 / 1.32) but noisier in the older bands. Within a band, years licensed correlates with exact age at 0.51 (17-24) to 0.95 (65+) in developed data. Emerging 17-24 drivers have years licensed with deciles 0 / 1 / 4. Mix: 17-24 is 19.6% of emerging training exposure against 13.5% developed, and 24.8% of motor test rows. 17-24 is also 24.7% of buildings test rows.
findings.method: Tweedie or Poisson GLMs on developed data (fit 2021-22, score 2023 raw cost), with 22 fine age bands against the 5 emerging bands. Relativities are band rate divided by the overall rate, using 2023-24 in each market. Correlation of age with years licensed by band (developed).
findings.implication: Banding is a minor loss. Inference: it likely reflects data minimisation or how the broker supplies data, not a ban on age rating. The banded Part 1 age curve is a sound prior, but the emerging young-driver loading is a little flatter (1.53 against 1.72). The heavier young mix in 2025 raises the expected motor cost on its own.
findings.adjustment: Average Part 1's exact-age curve within each emerging band (weighted by the developed age distribution) and use it as a credibility prior, shrinking towards emerging band estimates. Keep years licensed as a smooth term to recover detail within bands, especially for 17-24.

check.note: Developed data (fit 2021-22, score 2023 raw cost), moving from 22 fine age bands to the 5 bands: Tweedie D2 -0.0012 in motor (0.0900 to 0.0888 against the unweighted-mean baseline, which the stated 0.0856 and 0.0844 also use) and Poisson -0.0018. Contents loses 0.0002. Buildings improves 0.0017 (stated 0.0023), because fine bands overfit. Motor frequency relativity to the overall 2023-24 rate, developed against emerging: 1.72/1.53, 1.10/1.06, 0.81/0.78, 0.72/0.72, 0.91/0.89. Contents at 17-24: 1.31/1.32. Developed correlation of age with years licensed within band: 0.51, 0.75, 0.87, 0.87, 0.95. Emerging 17-24 years licensed at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentiles: 0, 1, 4. Share of exposure aged 17-24: 19.6% emerging, 13.5% developed. Test rows aged 17-24: 24.8% motor, 24.7% buildings (and 24.7% contents). One nuance: each relativity is to its own market's overall rate, and emerging's heavier young mix pulls its 17-24 relativity down. Relative to the 35-49 band the young loading is 2.12 developed against 1.96 emerging, so the flattening is about 8% rather than 11%.

findings.title: Other regulatory signals: telematics and mileage removed (the biggest information loss); claims-handling regime and discount rules unchanged
findings.evidence: Fact: emerging motor has no annual_mileage, telematics_opt_in or telematics_score. On developed data, adding banded mileage and telematics to an emerging-style motor GLM raises Tweedie D2 from 0.0863 to 0.1002 (+0.014), more than ten times the loss from age banding or credit. Claims handling is the same in both markets. Recoveries: own damage 21.6% of incurred in emerging against 21.8% developed, theft 3.6% against 3.7%, none on bodily injury, third-party property or glass. Repudiation: motor 1.5% against 1.2%, contents 1.3% against 1.3%, buildings 0 in both. Excesses are identical (compulsory 250 motor and 350 home; voluntary menu 0/250/500/1,000). Insurer-declined renewals: 0.5% against 0.7%. The discount rules are the same in both markets: 5% for every direct row, 10% only for new business through comparison sites, 0 otherwise.
findings.method: Schema comparison. Developed GLM with and without banded mileage and telematics (fit 2021-22, score 2023). Recovery share and repudiation rate by peril and line for 2023-24 losses. Cross-tabulation of discount by channel and new business in both markets.
findings.implication: Inference: losing the telematics data is consistent with privacy rules or an immature market. It is a structural limit on emerging motor accuracy: expect a motor D2 well below Part 1's 0.083. Part of the gender effect may stand in for the missing mileage, but that cannot be tested. Because the claims regime is unchanged, Part 1's treatment of excess, recoveries and repudiated claims carries over as it is. A new-business-only comparison-site discount would conflict with UK-style rules against renewal customers paying more than new ones (FCA GIPP). That bears on the premium charged, not the scored cost.
findings.adjustment: Carry over Part 1's target definition (net of recoveries, repudiated claims excluded) unchanged. Set expectations and uncertainty for the lower motor accuracy. No mileage or telematics proxy is available to build.

check.note: The claims-regime facts are confirmed. Recovery share of incurred, 2023-24: own damage 21.7% emerging against 21.8% developed; theft 3.5% against 3.7%; zero on bodily injury, third-party property and glass. Repudiation: motor 1.5% against 1.2%; contents 1.3% against 1.3%; buildings 0 in both. Compulsory excess is 250 (motor) and 350 (home), and the voluntary menu is 0/250/500/1,000 in both markets. Insurer-declined renewals are 0.46% against 0.65%, but that is the motor figure only: across all lines it is 0.33% against 0.46%. Discount rules are identical in both markets, on training and test rows: direct 5%, comparison-site new business 10%, 0 otherwise. The size of the telematics loss is overstated, as set out below.
check.corrected_evidence: Adding banded mileage and telematics to the emerging-style developed motor GLM (fit 2021-22, score 2023) gains +0.0139 to +0.0145 in Tweedie D2, matching the stated +0.014. However, 0.0090 of that comes from one row, the 11.89m bodily injury claim: the telematics model predicts 968 for that row instead of 685. Excluding that row, the gain is +0.0058, against +0.0011 for fine age bands and +0.0005 for credit band on the same basis. In Poisson frequency, which the large claim does not affect, the gain is +0.0076 against +0.0018 for age bands. Mileage and telematics are still the largest information loss, but about 4-10 times the others, not more than ten times.

findings.title: 'Costs are different': claim severity is about 0.6x developed for motor and about 0.7-0.8x for home (fire excepted), at the same sums insured and excesses
findings.evidence: Median net severity ratio, emerging / developed (2023-24 losses). Motor: own damage 0.62, third-party property 0.63, theft 0.58, glass 0.66, bodily injury 0.62; the ratio is roughly constant from the 10th to the 90th percentile (0.54 to 0.74). Buildings: escape of water 0.71, storm 0.71, flood 0.72, subsidence 0.66, accidental damage 0.75, but fire 1.03 (and 1.4 at the 90th percentile). Contents: accidental damage 0.70, escape of water 0.79, flood 0.78, theft 0.81. Exposure is otherwise matched: buildings sum insured quantiles are almost identical (median 229k in both), contents median 35.8k against 39.7k, the same excess structure, and vehicle value group 10.9 against 11.0 (vehicles are older: 10.3 years against 8.5). Motor frequency is higher on every peril (x1.23 to x1.55 in 2023), so motor cost per unit of exposure is 433 / 383 (2023 / 2024) against 587 developed in 2023. Emerging tail: 10 motor claims over 50k (0.14% of claims, against 0.37% developed) and a maximum of 156k. Buildings has 33 claims over 50k and 16 over 100k. Claims over 100k are 40% of 2023 emerging buildings cost and 25% of 2024. Fire cost per unit of exposure is 283 (2023) and 93 (2024), against 99 developed.
findings.method: Per-peril quantiles of net incurred (repudiated claims excluded) for 2023-24 losses in each market, plus approximate gross cost (net plus the row's excesses). Distributions of sum insured, excess and vehicle variables. Peril frequencies on recomputed exposure.
findings.implication: Inference: repair and labour costs are lower (partial losses scale down), while fire losses, which track rebuild value or sum insured, do not. Part 1's severity levels, its 50k large-claim threshold and its Pareto scale cannot be reused in CU terms. The shape of the severity distribution transfers reasonably well as a multiplicative rescaling. The 12% cat load and the fire volatility point the same way.
findings.adjustment: Rebase severity by line and peril to emerging data: motor about x0.62, home about x0.70-0.80, fire about x1.0. Scale the motor large-claim threshold to about 30k (50k x 0.62). For buildings, give fire its own treatment (pooled or credibility-weighted towards a long-run level), and widen the buildings range to reflect the year-to-year fire swing.

check.note: Median net severity, emerging/developed (2023-24 losses, repudiated excluded). Motor: own damage 0.62, third-party property 0.63, theft 0.58, glass 0.66, bodily injury 0.62; 0.54 to 0.74 from the 10th to the 90th percentile. Buildings: escape of water 0.71, storm 0.71, flood 0.72, subsidence 0.66, accidental damage 0.75, fire 1.03 (1.42 at the 90th percentile). Contents: accidental damage 0.70, escape of water 0.79, flood 0.78, theft 0.81. Buildings sum insured percentiles (10/50/90) are 124k/229k/365k against 124k/229k/364k. Contents median is 35.8k against 39.6k (stated 39.7k). Vehicle value group 10.87 against 11.0; vehicle age 10.25 against 8.49. Motor peril frequency ratios in 2023 run x1.23 to x1.55. Motor cost per unit of exposure is 433/383 against 587 developed in 2023. Emerging motor has 10 claims over 50k (0.14%, against 0.37% developed) and a maximum of 155.7k. Buildings has 33 claims over 50k and 16 over 100k. Claims over 100k are 39.5% of 2023 buildings cost and 24.6% of 2024. Fire cost per unit of exposure is 283 and 93, against 94-105 developed. Reporting lags are similar (motor bodily injury mean 164 against 153 days), so differences in maturity do not drive the ratios.

findings.title: Emerging claims inflation cannot be estimated from two years; Part 1's trend is the only usable prior
findings.evidence: Like-for-like median net severity, 2024 against 2023 (short-tail perils, losses January to September, reported within 60 days). Emerging: motor -4.9% (bootstrap 95% CI -12.7% to +6.0%, n = 2,369 / 2,550), buildings +3.7% (-19% to +35%), contents +3.8% (-27% to +43%). Developed, on the same filter: motor +3.6% (0.0% to +7.5%), buildings +5.0%, contents +3.7%, in line with the Part 1 fitted trends of +3.8%, +5.3% and +4.2% a year. Written premium went up 3-5% from 2024 to 2025 in each emerging motor age band (developed: +3.2% to +3.4%).
findings.method: Median ratio with 1,000 independent bootstrap resamples of each year's claims. Same filter in both markets to remove reporting-maturity bias.
findings.implication: Two years cannot separate an emerging-specific inflation rate from noise. The emerging motor point estimate is negative but consistent with Part 1's +3.8%. 'Different costs' is established for the level, not for the trend.
findings.adjustment: Project 2025 with Part 1's line trends (about +4% to +5% a year) as a prior, cap emerging-only trend fits, and put trend uncertainty (for example plus or minus 5 points a year) explicitly into the 2025 level range.

check.note: Losses January to September, reported within 60 days, 1,000 bootstrap draws. Emerging motor, excluding bodily injury: -4.9% (CI -13.1% to +5.7%; n = 2,369/2,550). Buildings (accidental damage, escape of water, storm): +3.7% (-19.5% to +34.8%). Contents (accidental damage, escape of water, theft): +3.8% (-25.9% to +44.0%). Developed, same filter: motor +3.6%, buildings +5.0%, contents +3.7%. Written premium 2025 against 2024 by emerging motor age band: +3.2% to +5.3%; developed +3.2% to +3.3%. The figures depend on the peril set: home excludes flood and fire, and the finding does not say so. Including them turns emerging buildings to -3.6% and contents to -6.0%, and developed buildings to +6.9% and contents to +1.3%. That strengthens the conclusion that two years cannot identify an emerging trend.

findings.title: The insurer's current emerging pricing is the developed tariff ported unchanged; it is a strong compact prior for relativities but needs re-levelling
findings.evidence: 2024 written premium by driver age band, emerging / developed: 1,133 / 1,147, 472 / 477, 458 / 463, 461 / 463, 536 / 539 CU, all within about 1%. Discount rules are identical in both markets. Loss ratio on written premium (undeveloped, exposure-weighted), emerging 2023 / 2024: motor 0.71 / 0.63 (developed 1.04 / 0.78), contents 0.73 / 0.66 (0.84 / 0.80), buildings 1.49 / 0.83 (1.30 / 1.29). Elasticity of cost to log written premium matches developed: motor 0.85 (SE 0.10) against 0.83, buildings 0.80 (0.14) against 0.81, contents 1.04 (0.14) against 0.98. Motor frequency elasticity is lower, at 0.78 (0.03) against 0.92 (0.01). As a single predictor, log written premium beats a one-year GLM on every rating factor out of time (Tweedie D2, 2023 to 2024 / 2024 to 2023): motor 0.066 / 0.028 against at best 0.063 / 0.013; buildings 0.070 / 0.068 against -0.017 / 0.016; contents 0.064 / 0.060 against 0.065 / 0.045. Written premium is in all three test files.
findings.method: Average written premium by band in both markets. Loss ratio as cost over written premium times exposure. Tweedie or Poisson GLM of claims on log written premium with an exposure offset. Out-of-time comparison against ridge GLMs on the full factor set (best of ridge 10 to 10,000).
findings.implication: Inference: written premium encodes Part 1's relativity structure, which carries over well apart from the overall level and a somewhat flatter motor frequency gradient. That makes it a ready-made carrier of what transfers from Part 1. Part 1 excluded it (no gain with four years of data); in sparse emerging data it is valuable. Because the tariff is gender-neutral and carries no emerging cost level, it must be re-levelled (motor about 0.65-0.70 of the tariff level) and complemented with gender and emerging-specific effects.
findings.adjustment: Use log written premium (or Part 1 model scores) as an offset or prior, with emerging-fitted level, slope and corrections (gender if adopted, region, fire), and test against a pure emerging GLM with both-year validation. Do not read written premium as a gross premium: it sits near risk cost in the developed data (loss ratio about 1.0 for motor), so expense loads cannot be backed out of it.

check.note: Confirmed: 2024 written premium by band 1,133/1,147, 472/477, 458/463, 461/463, 536/539. Loss ratios on written premium x exposure, 2023/2024: emerging motor 0.71/0.63 (developed 1.04/0.78), contents 0.73/0.66 (0.84/0.80), buildings 1.49/0.83 (1.30/1.29). Elasticity of cost to log written premium: motor 0.853 (SE 0.103) against 0.830; buildings 0.804 (0.136) against 0.808; contents 1.044 (0.141) against 0.976. Motor frequency elasticity 0.781 (0.026) against 0.921 (0.010). Part 1 kept written premium out (D-05). The D2 levels and the re-levelling factor need correcting, as set out below.
check.corrected_evidence: The D2 levels use the unweighted-mean baseline (Part 1's models.d2_tweedie), which credits the exposure offset alone. Against that baseline, an exposure-only model already scores 0.052 (motor, 2023 to 2024), 0.045 and 0.030 (contents) and 0.025 (buildings, 2024 to 2023). Against the constant-rate x exposure baseline, which python/emerging.py labels the leaderboard's, written-premium-only D2 is: motor 0.015/0.029, buildings 0.070/0.044, contents 0.019/0.031. The project uses both definitions, so the baseline should be stated. The ranking against a full GLM does not depend on the baseline. In my replication written premium wins 5 of 6 cases; motor 2023 to 2024 is the exception, where the ridge GLM's 0.0161 edges 0.0152. 'Beats on every factor' is therefore close but depends on the specification. Re-levelling: 0.65-0.70 comes from undeveloped loss ratios. Emerging motor reporting is as slow as developed: bodily injury mean lag 164 against 153 days, and its share of incurred falls from 32% (2023) to 25% (2024). Applying Part 1's motor development factors (x1.029 for 2023, x1.236 for 2024) gives developed loss ratios of about 0.73 and 0.78. That is an inference, because emerging development cannot be observed. The motor re-level should therefore be about 0.73-0.78 of tariff, not 0.65-0.70, before any 2025 trend or tariff change.
